title: Each sentence is within the maximum applicable at the date of offending
statement: Misidentifying the maximum is appealable error unless immaterial. For offences before a change in penalty the court applies any reduction but never an increase, except that where the maximum was reduced and then increased again before sentence the court may sentence under the original maximum if the current one is of the same magnitude or higher. Counsel must check the maximum, and the parties’ agreement on it does not bind the court.
test: For every charge: (1) look up the offence in the offence register and select the maxima entry whose [from, to] contains the offence date(s); if no entry contains the date, the Manual is silent for it — mark the maximum unresolved and ask the user (never interpolate between printed periods); a date range straddling a change is unresolved too. (2) Apply a later reduction, never a later increase — except where the maximum was reduced and then increased again before sentence and the current maximum is of the same magnitude or higher: a sentence within the original maximum then passes → caution. (3) Apply a conditional maximum only if its condition is established on the facts (criminal organisation, within 500 metres of a school, face covering); where the register marks the conditional maximum with a caution (s 71AC and s 71B “within 500 metres of a school”: whether the supply or trafficking must be to a child is stated inconsistently, flag.school_500m_condition) apply it only when the user confirms the statutory condition — otherwise unresolved → caution. (4) Relative maxima: equal_to_primary (and “accumulated maxima” where the row is marked multiple_offences: the sum of the primary maxima), greater_of_primary_and_stated (stated_years) and fraction_of_primary (factor 0.6) are computed from the primary offence’s maximum, which the user must identify; equal_to_intended_offence needs the intended offence; table_not_reproduced, lower_penalty_in_other_enactment and law_of_place_capped_at_life cannot be resolved from the Manual (ask the user). Crimes Act s 321C(1)(c) conspiracy to commit an offence punishable by life (other than murder or treason, and not covered by DPCS s 79): operative maximum 15 years (fn 4805) → error above it; s 321I(1)(c) incitement likewise, but a sentence above 15 years → caution, not error (fn 4807 speaks of conspiracy: flag.inchoate_life_maximum_footnotes; guide.inchoate.maxima_notes). (4a) at_large rows (penalty_scale rules scale.at_large, scale.at_large_guidance): there is no numeric ceiling, but the sentence must not be “inordinate” and may be guided by the maximum for similar statutory offending → caution. (5) current_only rows print no dates: for offending that may pre-date the current maximum → caution. (6) Fines: natural person ≤ the printed maximum (pu_individual / fine_penalty_units); where only a term is printed, “generally” 10 penalty units per month of the maximum term (scale.fine_alternative) — but no such fine where the maximum is life, and for Level 2 only in addition to imprisonment (scale.level2_fine_additional_only; audit.fine_rules); a dollar figure is converted at the penalty unit value for the offence date (scale.penalty_unit_at_offence) (offending on or after 1 July 2026 → caution, flag.penalty_unit_values_end_2025); body corporate ≤ pu_company where printed; where none is printed, above five times the natural-person maximum → error for any offence (12.2; unless the user identifies a provision setting a higher company maximum: caution, app policy), and for an offence outside the Crimes Act a fine above the natural-person maximum but not above five times it → caution, unresolved (5.1.1 states the multiplier only for Crimes Act offences: flag.body_corporate_fine_multiplier). (7) Ceiling adjustments: a Victorian summary offence ≤ min(maximum, 24 months); a CCE offender sentenced for a CCE offence ≤ min(2 × maximum term, 25 years), except that where CCE status rests on a rolled-up count whose largest transaction is exactly $50,000 a sentence above the ordinary maximum but within that ceiling → caution, not error (flag.cce_value_threshold) (the output records that fact → caution if it does not; uniform but different penalties for CCE and non-CCE offences without explanation → caution); no ceiling applies to an indefinite sentence (checked by its own gate); a statutory offence with no maximum specified is presumptively 2 years; a fine-only offence admits no imprisonment. (8) Compare each individual sentence (term, fine) with the result → error if it exceeds it; where the printed level and the printed term disagree, error above the higher figure and unresolved (caution) between the two (audit.level_term_mismatch); mark unresolved where the maximum cannot be determined; surface any register note, flag or confidence below “high”.
logic: for c in charges: m = maximum(c.offence_id, c.offence_dates, facts) -> None if no period contains the date (unresolved); apply reduced-then-increased exception; apply conditional/relative/at_large rules; m = 180 months for a Crimes Act s 321C(1)(c) conspiracy to commit an offence punishable by life (not murder or treason, not DPCS s 79) (error above); s 321I(1)(c) incitement likewise, but above 180 months → caution (flag.inchoate_life_maximum_footnotes); m = min(m, 24 months) if Victorian summary offence; m = min(2*m, 300 months) if cce.regime applies (CCE status resting on a rolled-up count whose largest transaction is exactly $50,000: a sentence above the ordinary maximum but within the CCE ceiling → caution, flag.cce_value_threshold); assert c.months <= max(level_term, printed_term) (caution between them); natural person: assert c.fine_pu <= m.fine_pu; body corporate: assert c.fine_pu <= (m.pu_company if printed else 5 × m.fine_pu) (caution instead where the user identifies a higher company maximum: app policy), and if not printed and not crimes_act and c.fine_pu > m.fine_pu: caution (flag.body_corporate_fine_multiplier)

title: Penalty level and printed term disagree
statement: Where a description in years or months is inconsistent with a penalty level, the level prevails unless there is a contrary intention. The Manual itself prints some level/term pairs that do not match the scale. Maxima for periods before 1 September 1997 use level/term pairs that do not follow the current table, and the Manual does not set out the scale then in force.

title: Magistrates’ Court jurisdictional limits
statement: Victorian summary offences: maximum two years’ imprisonment. Indictable offences heard summarily: two years per offence; cumulative terms for offences committed at the same time not over five years; fines up to 500 penalty units (2500 for a body corporate; 12.2 states the 2500-unit limit for a body corporate in any matter heard summarily). The limit is jurisdictional only. The Drug Court Division of the Magistrates’ Court is subject to the same limits.
test: Any court: a Victorian summary offence ≤ min(its maximum, 24 months) → error. If court ∈ {Magistrates’ Court, Drug Court (MC)}: each term ≤ 24 months → error; total cumulative term for Victorian offences committed at the same time (charges[].same_time_group, from intake.charges) ≤ 60 months → error; where the user identifies an Act expressly providing otherwise → caution, citing that Act; which offences were committed at the same time unknown and the total over 60 months → unresolved, caution (ask the user); each fine ≤ its maximum (for a body corporate, as fixed by audit.fine_rules) → error; a natural person’s fine for an indictable offence ≤ 500 penalty units → error; a body corporate’s fine in any matter heard summarily ≤ 2500 penalty units → error (12.2). An aggregate sentence over 24 months in the Magistrates’ Court → caution, unresolved (flag.mc_aggregate_over_two_years).
logic: if summary_offence: assert c.months <= min(max, 24); if court in ('MC', 'DrugCourt-MC'): assert all(c.months <= 24); for g in same_time_groups: assert effective_months(g) <= 60 (error) unless express_act (then caution) (the group’s cumulative term: its base term plus the parts cumulated within it, not the sum of the terms); if same_time_group unknown and tes_months > 60: caution; each fine <= its maximum (body corporate: as in audit.fine_rules); natural person, indictable offence: fine <= 500 pu; body corporate, any matter heard summarily: fine <= 2500 pu; if aggregate and aggregate.months > 24: caution

title: Category 1 and Category 2 offences: imprisonment without a CCO (subject to the exceptions)
statement: For most Category 1 offences the court must imprison and not attach a CCO; the exception is for Category 1 offences that are also mandatory minimum offences against protected officials. For Category 2 offences it must imprison (without a CCO) unless a listed exception is established; the residual “substantial and compelling, exceptional and rare” exception is stringent. A special reason is an exception the mandatory minimum provisions provide (9.1.3): for a Category 1 offence with no mandatory minimum it does not exist.
test: For each charge whose register row shows Category 1 or 2 for the offence date (on or after 20 March 2017) and the category condition as printed in the register row: Category 1 — imprisonment without a CCO passes; otherwise → error, except: (a) ss 16, 17 or 18 against a protected official (and, per fn 2005, ss 317AC/317AD when the user confirms their Category 1 status: flag.driving_protected_category1) with a special reason found: imprisonment without a CCO, or a mandatory treatment and monitoring order, Residential Treatment Order or Court Secure Treatment Order on the 9.1.2.3 conditions, passes; an MTMO combined with imprisonment → caution, unresolved (flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); (b) ss 16, 17 or 18 against a protected official (not gross violence), offender under 21 at sentence, no special reason, pre-sentence report finding: a youth justice centre order of at least the minimum passes; (c) ss 15A/15B against a protected official with a special reason found: imprisonment without a CCO passes; any other disposition → caution, unresolved (flag.gross_violence_protected_special_reason); (d) any other Category 1 offence that carries a mandatory minimum non-parole period (register minimum_non_parole: ss 15A/15B where the victim is not a protected official, ss 77B, 79A) with a special reason found and any disposition other than imprisonment without a CCO (a non-custodial disposition, or imprisonment combined with a CCO) → caution, unresolved (flag.category1_special_reason); a Category 1 offence that carries no mandatory minimum (e.g. murder, rape, ss 49A, 49J, 50C, 50D, DPCSA ss 71, 72) with a non-custodial disposition → error whatever reason is given (a special reason is the exception the mandatory minimum provisions provide: 9.1.3). Category 2 — imprisonment without a CCO passes; an exception identified with its evidential basis passes (the offender proves (b)/(c) on the balance of probabilities); otherwise → error. A youth justice centre order on a Category 1 or 2 charge outside route (b) → caution (flag.category_imprisonment_vs_custodial). Historic provisions with no register row (cat1.historic_sexual_provisions: 24.1.6.2 rows marked “#”): an adult offender and offending from 20 March to 30 June 2017 → treat as Category 1 as above once the user confirms the provision; unconfirmed → caution.
logic: for c in charges: if c.category is None and c.historic_provision in cat1.historic_sexual_provisions: c.category = 1 if (c.historic_provision_confirmed and age_at_offence >= 18 and 2017-03-20 <= offence_date <= 2017-06-30) else caution; if c.category == 1: ok = (c.type == 'imprisonment' and not c.cco_combination) or (c.offence in (s16, s17, s18, s317AC, s317AD) and c.protected_official and c.special_reason and c.type in ('mtmo', 'rto', 'csto') and not c.cco_combination) or (c.offence in (s16, s17, s18) and c.protected_official and c.type == 'yjc' and age_sentence < 21 and not c.special_reason and c.yjc_months >= c.min_npp_months); elif c.type == 'yjc': caution; elif c.offence in (s15A, s15B) and c.special_reason: caution; elif c.offence in (s16, s17, s18, s317AC, s317AD) and c.protected_official and c.special_reason and c.type == 'mtmo' and c.cco_combination: caution (flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); elif c.special_reason and c.has_mandatory_minimum and c.offence not in (s16, s17, s18, s317AC, s317AD): caution (flag.category1_special_reason); else error. if c.category == 2: ok = (c.type == 'imprisonment' and not c.cco_combination) or c.cat2_exception; elif c.type == 'yjc': caution; else error

title: Mandatory minimum non-parole periods and terms
statement: For the five groups (manslaughter, gross violence, protected officials, driving against protected officials, aggravated home invasion or carjacking) the court must impose imprisonment with at least the minimum non-parole period unless an exclusion applies (under 18 at the offence; the accessory rules stated for each group; the protected-official youth justice centre alternative) or a special reason is found and recorded in writing.

Check the exclusions (under 18 at offence; accessory rules as stated for each group). → error if the non-parole period (or term) is below the minimum without an identified special reason, its evidential basis and the statement that it is recorded in writing — except: ss 16, 17 or 18 against a protected official (not ss 15A/15B), offender under 21 at sentence, no special reason found, the pre-sentence report finding made: a youth justice centre order of a term not less than the minimum passes. If a special reason is relied on for ss 16, 17, 18, 317AC or 317AD against a protected official → error unless the disposition is imprisonment without a CCO or a mandatory treatment and monitoring order, Residential Treatment Order or Court Secure Treatment Order on the stated conditions; imprisonment combined with a mandatory treatment and monitoring order → caution, unresolved (flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); for ss 15A/15B against a protected official with a special reason, any disposition other than imprisonment without a CCO → caution, unresolved (flag.gross_violence_protected_special_reason). Aggravated home invasion / carjacking with multiple charges: an overall npp ≥ 3 years passes, but where the individual sentence on the aggravated charge is under 3 years 6 months → caution (flag.aggravated_hi_cj_multiple_charge_guidepost). title: Non-parole period rules
statement: Imprisonment of two years or more requires a non-parole period unless inappropriate; none may be fixed if the total is under 12 months; it must be at least six months shorter than the total; standard sentence offences require at least 30 years (life), 70% or 60% unless not in the interests of justice (with reasons); an offender serving the non-parole period of a prior sentence gets a new single non-parole period; an unusual non-parole period should be explained.
test: tes ≥ 24 months (not indefinite) → npp present or a stated reason it is inappropriate (error); indefinite sentence → no npp (error); tes < 12 months → no npp (error); npp ≤ tes − 6 months (error); imprisonment combined with a CCO and 12 < term < 24 months → no npp (error; exactly 12 months: caution, flag.npp_cco_twelve_months); a charge passing sso.scope → npp ≥ 30 years (life) / 70% (term over 20 years) / 60% (term under 20 years; exactly 20 years: 60% floor with a caution below 70%) unless interests-of-justice reasons are given (error), unresolved (caution) where the floor cannot be reconciled with the 12-month and six-month rules, and the output states the “relevant term” used (an assumption: the total effective sentence). New single npp: required where the offender is serving the npp of a prior sentence of imprisonment, not where the prior sentence was a straight sentence or its npp is complete, and not merely because the offender is sentenced at one time on several indictments; the output states its commencement date; if it commences from the date of the new sentence, the allowance for the parole sentence already served is stated; it must not make the offender eligible for parole earlier than without the new sentence; no “overall minimum term”; no double-counted pre-sentence detention (error for each). npp outside 60–75% of tes → reasons present (caution only, and not for head sentences of about 10 years or more, where the range ceases to be of much guidance).

title: CCO availability, duration, combination and condition limits
statement: A CCO requires an offence punishable by more than five penalty units, a pre-sentence report (unless only unpaid work of 300 hours or less), and consent. Duration limits: Magistrates’ Court two/four/five years by number of offences; higher courts five years; cumulative CCOs five years. A combination sentence’s imprisonment cannot exceed one year after pre-sentence detention (except arson). Conditions: at least one Division 4 or justice plan condition, none for restitution, compensation, costs or damages; unpaid work up to 600 hours; curfew two to 12 hours a day for up to six months; electronic monitoring only in the higher courts and only for a curfew or place exclusion. No CCO with a youth justice centre order, and none on a Category 1/2 charge except through the Chapter 9 exception routes.
test: For each CCO in the proposal: (1) availability — offence maximum fine > 5 penalty units; consent recorded (fact or stated assumption); pre-sentence report received unless the only condition is unpaid work under 300 hours → error; work-only CCO of exactly 300 hours without a report → caution (flag.cco_work_only_300_hours). (2) duration — Magistrates’ Court ≤ 24 / 48 / 60 months by the number of offences the CCO covers; Supreme/County Court ≤ 60; CCOs cumulated (including on any CCO in force) ≤ 60 in total → error. (3) combination — not arson: Σ imprisonment − pre-sentence detention ≤ 12 months → error; arson in the Supreme/County Court: no combination ceiling; arson in the Magistrates’ Court: > 24 months → error, 12–24 months → caution (flag.cco_arson_combination); no CCO on an excluded offence (a charge the user marks excluded, or a Category 1/2 charge that limb (6) errors) → error; a CCO on a Category 1/2 charge that limb (6) passes or cautions on an exception route (a Category 2 exception established; an MTMO on route (a); a special reason on route (c) or (d)) → caution, not error (“excluded offence” is undefined: flag.cco_excluded_offence_undefined; an MTMO with imprisonment: flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); a charge that may be excluded but is not Category 1/2 → caution (flag.cco_excluded_offence_undefined). (4) conditions — at least one Division 4 or justice plan condition, and no restitution/compensation/costs/damages condition → error; unpaid work ≤ 600 hours with the hours and the completion period stated → error; with another CCO in force or cumulated, total hours > 600 → caution (flag.cco_hours_maximum_time_limits); curfew 2–12 h/day and ≤ 6 months → error; electronic monitoring only if court ∈ {Supreme, County}, only to monitor a curfew or place/area exclusion condition, and for no longer than that condition → error; justice plan condition < 24 months and ≤ the CCO → error; residence, place or curfew conditions possibly inconsistent with an existing FVIO, PSIO or child protection order (intake) → caution. (5) youth detention — a CCO combined with a YJC order on the same charge → error; a YRC order with a CCO, or a CCO on one charge with a YJC order on another → caution (flag.yjc_combination_wording). (6) Category 1/2 — a CCO on a Category 1 charge → error, except: an MTMO on route (a) of audit.category_1_2 passes, and an MTMO combined with imprisonment on that route → caution (flag.mtmo_combination_sentence); a CCO, alone or combined with imprisonment, that audit.category_1_2 makes a caution on route (c) or (d) → caution, not error (flag.gross_violence_protected_special_reason; flag.category1_special_reason). A CCO on a Category 2 charge without an established exception → error (the Category 2 exception passes). (7) MTMO — the CCO has a judicial monitoring condition and a treatment and rehabilitation condition or a justice plan condition → error otherwise. (8) a non-parole period with a CCO is checked by audit.non_parole_rules. (9) commencement (runs only on a commencement the proposal states: disposition.cco.commencement) — a CCO not combined with imprisonment: a stated commencement more than three months after the order → error; a CCO combined with imprisonment: commencement before the offender’s release → error, and the three-month limit does not apply to it (2.4.7 “However”; sentence.commencement_rules).

title: Aggregate sentence availability and ceiling
statement: An aggregate sentence is available for two or more offences founded on the same facts or forming (part of) a series of offences of the same or similar character; it cannot be imposed on a serious offender for a relevant offence, if any offence is a standard sentence offence, or for a mix of parole-violation and other-time offences; it cannot exceed the total of separate sentences; the decision, reasons and effect must be announced. It may be inappropriate in some circumstances, though not necessarily erroneous.
test: If the proposal uses an aggregate sentence: fewer than two offences → error; the joinder-type test (same facts or a series of the same or similar character) not addressed with reasons → caution; any member offence passes sso.scope → error (a standard-sentence-type offence outside the scheme → caution; a standard sentence offence sentenced in the same proceeding but outside the aggregate → caution, since the Manual’s “if one or more of the offences” is not limited to members); the offender is a serious offender and any offence is a relevant offence → error; a parole-violation offence mixed with other-time offences → error; the aggregate exceeds the total effective sentence that separate sentences could have produced (at most the sum of the separate maxima, and in the Magistrates’ Court within its cumulative cap) → error; a Magistrates’ Court aggregate over 24 months → caution; the output does not state the decision, reasons and effect → error; an aggregate used where the Manual says it may be inappropriate (few counts, scrutiny precluded, markedly disparate gravity) → caution.
logic: if aggregate: assert len(aggregate.charges) >= 2; assert not any(sso_in_scope) and not (serious_offender and any(relevant)) and not parole_mix; assert aggregate.months <= notional_tes <= sum(max_i); assert aggregate.announced and aggregate.reasons and aggregate.effect; if court == MC and aggregate.months > 24: caution

title: A sentence for each charge; base sentence and cumulation; time served declared
statement: A sentence must be imposed for each offence (unless aggregate); cumulation and concurrency should be made by reference to a base sentence, ordinarily the most severe; the head sentence and any non-parole period stated; time already served declared and noted (nil days where the court otherwise orders, for good reason).
test: Every charge has a disposition (or belongs to an aggregate) → error; the total effective sentence equals base + cumulated parts (consistency) → error; the base is not the longest individual sentence → caution (cum.base_sentence); no cumulation onto a life sentence — whether the offender is paroled from it or is already sentenced to or serving it (21.4.1: further imprisonment only concurrently) → error; a life sentence imposed on another charge in this sentencing: a term cumulated on it → caution (app reading of “already sentenced to”: cum.life_parole); pre-sentence detention is stated in days (or recorded as unknown), counting the whole continuous custody from arrest where that rule applies and excluding non-declarable periods → error; where the court “otherwise orders”, the declaration is nil days, never because a combination sentence is intended → error; no good reason stated for the order → caution (8.6.1: the discretion “should not be exercised without good reason”); if the offender is serving a Commonwealth sentence: the commencement date of the new term is directed no later than the s 16(4) point, and no order cumulates the Victorian term on the Commonwealth sentence (there is no power) → error; a commencement date earlier than that point → caution (2.4.7 says “immediately after”; flag.cth_sentence_commencement_fixed_or_latest).

title: Section 6AAA statement of the sentence that would have been imposed but for the plea
statement: Where a less severe sentence is imposed because of a guilty plea and the sentence is a custodial order, imprisonment, a CCO of two years or more, a fine over 10 penalty units or an aggregate fine over 20 penalty units, the notional sentence (and notional non-parole period) must be stated for the overall sentence and recorded. The plea may change the form of the sentence itself, so the notional sentence may be of a different (more severe) type. Failure is an irregularity that does not of itself invalidate the sentence.
test: If any plea is guilty, the reasoning gives the plea weight (a less severe sentence), and the disposition is imprisonment, a CCO of 24 months or more, a fine over 10 penalty units or an aggregate fine over 20 penalty units: → error unless the output states a notional sentence for the overall sentence (type and, where it has one, length) and, if a non-parole period is fixed, a notional non-parole period. Compare by the type’s measure: if the notional type is the same as the actual type — imprisonment: notional term ≥ actual term and notional npp ≥ npp, with at least one strictly greater; CCO: notional months and unpaid-work hours each ≥ actual, with at least one strictly greater → pass; both equal → pass only if the reasoning states which other conditions the plea reduced, otherwise caution (app policy); one greater and the other smaller → caution (app policy: severity not settled); notional lower on one and not higher on the other → error; fine or aggregate fine: notional amount (penalty units or dollars) > actual; if the type differs, the notional type must be more severe in the ordering of principle.sentence_type_ordering (no month comparison) → error otherwise; a comparison that ordering does not settle → caution. Other custodial orders (youth detention, CSTO, RTO, DATO custodial part) → caution if no statement (flag.s6aaa_custodial_order_undefined). Pleas to some but not all charges → a notional total effective sentence is still sought, but a missing or odd figure → caution (flag.s6aaa_mixed_pleas). Other sentence forms → caution recommending the statement, never an error (flag.s6aaa_scope_2_4_9_vs_7_1_4). The figures stated are always the notional (undiscounted) ones.
logic: if plea_discount and triggers_6aaa(disposition): assert s6aaa.notional_type; if s6aaa.notional_type == disposition.type: if type == 'imprisonment': assert s6aaa.notional_tes_months >= total_effective_months and (not npp_months or s6aaa.notional_npp_months >= npp_months) and (s6aaa.notional_tes_months > total_effective_months or (npp_months and s6aaa.notional_npp_months > npp_months)); if type == 'cco': dm, dh = s6aaa.notional_cco_months - months, (s6aaa.notional_unpaid_hours or 0) - (unpaid_hours or 0); error if (dm <= 0 and dh <= 0 and (dm < 0 or dh < 0)); pass if dm >= 0 and dh >= 0 and (dm > 0 or dh > 0); if dm == 0 and dh == 0: pass if s6aaa.conditions_reduced else caution; else caution; if type in ('fine', 'aggregate_fine'): assert s6aaa.notional_fine_pu > fine_pu; else: r = compare(s6aaa.notional_type, disposition.type) (principle.sentence_type_ordering; None when unsettled); if r is None: caution; else assert r > 0; if mixed_pleas: downgrade to caution

title: Section 5(2AB): announcing a less severe sentence for cooperation
statement: If a court imposes a less severe sentence because the offender has undertaken to assist the authorities, it must announce that it is doing so and have the undertaking’s details recorded. statement: A magistrate who indicated a sentence of a particular type must not impose a more severe type (but may impose a less severe one); a higher court that gave an indication must not impose a more severe sentence type, or a longer total effective sentence, than indicated. title: Fines: availability by level, maximum, body corporate, aggregate fines
statement: No fine for Level 1; for Level 2 only in addition to imprisonment (natural person) unless otherwise stated; none where a dismissal, discharge or adjournment would serve. The maximum fine is in the provision, else follows the level; where the maximum is in years only, 10 penalty units per month; a body corporate up to five times. Fines for several offences are cumulative; an aggregate fine cannot exceed the sum of the maxima and is not available if any offence is a standard sentence offence.
test: For each fine: on a Level 1 offence → error, unless the offence row prints a fine (DPCSA ss 71, 72, 71AA criminal organisation), in which case → caution (fine ≤ the printed amount; flag.level1_fine_dpcsa); as an alternative to imprisonment for a Level 2 offence, natural person → error unless the offence provision states otherwise (ask the user; caution where the user says it does); a 25-year maximum printed without a level: a fine alone, or as an alternative to imprisonment, on a natural person → caution (the Manual does not say whether the Level 2 rule applies; a body corporate → no caution, 12.1); a life maximum printed without a level: no general fine (5.1.1; an unprinted fine is above the maximum), and a fine the row prints → caution (flag.fine_unlabelled_life_25_maximum); above the maximum (printed, else 10 × maximum months where only years are given) → error; body corporate: above the printed company maximum → error; where none is printed, above five times the natural-person maximum → error for any offence (unless the user identifies a provision setting a higher company maximum: caution, app policy), and for an offence outside the Crimes Act a fine above the natural-person maximum but not above five times it → caution (flag.body_corporate_fine_multiplier); offending on or after 1 July 2026 with a dollar conversion → caution (flag.penalty_unit_values_end_2025). Aggregate fine: fewer than two offences → error; the joinder test (same facts, or a series of offences of the same or similar character) not addressed → caution; above the sum of the maximum fines of its offences → error; any member offence passing sso.scope → error; a member offence that has a standard sentence but falls outside sso.scope → caution (flag.aggregate_fine_sso_test); separate fines are summed (no concurrency).
logic: for c in fines: if level == 1: error unless row.fine_printed (then caution); if level == 2 and natural_person and not with_imprisonment: error unless provision_states_otherwise (caution); if unlabelled_25 and natural_person and not with_imprisonment: caution (flag.fine_unlabelled_life_25_maximum); if unlabelled_life and row.fine_printed: caution (flag.fine_unlabelled_life_25_maximum); if body_corporate: {assert fine_pu <= (pu_company if printed else 5 * natural_max) (caution instead where the user identifies a higher company maximum: app policy); if not printed and not crimes_act and fine_pu > natural_max: caution (flag.body_corporate_fine_multiplier)} else (natural person): assert fine_pu <= max_fine (printed, else 10 × maximum months; none for life); if aggregate_fine: (caution if joinder test not addressed); assert len >= 2 and amount <= sum(max_fine_i) and not any(sso_in_scope); if any(has_standard_sentence and not sso_in_scope): caution (flag.aggregate_fine_sso_test)

refs.q: A fine can be imposed with or without conviction and may be imposed in addition to, or instead of, any other sentence. For Level 2 offences (punishable by 25 years’ imprisonment), a fine can only be imposed in addition to imprisonment. It cannot be imposed as an alternative, unless otherwise stated or if the offender is a body corporate. Lastly, a fine may not be imposed if the purposes for which a sentence is imposed can be achieved by dismissal, discharge, or adjournment.

title: Youth detention: age, prerequisites, serious youth offences, maximum, aggregate and custody
statement: A youth justice centre order is for offenders aged 15 to under 21 at sentence (youth residential centre under 15); it needs a pre-sentence report and a finding of reasonable prospects of rehabilitation or vulnerability in adult prison, and the court must consider the nature of the offence and the offender’s age, character and history; for Category A (or B with a prior) serious youth offences exceptional circumstances are required; maximum four years (higher courts) or two years (Magistrates’ Court) regardless of the number of convictions, also capping cumulation across occasions.
test: If YJC/YRC proposed: age at sentence (YJC 15 to under 21; YRC under 15) → error; pre-sentence report and the rehabilitation / impressionability finding recorded → error; Category A serious youth offence (or Category B with a prior Category A/B conviction) identified by the user → error unless an exceptional-circumstances finding is stated; category unknown → caution (flag.serious_youth_offence_categories); youth detention imposed now (YJC/YRC terms only; the effective period after concurrency and cumulation, not the sum of the terms) > 48 months (Supreme/County Court) or 24 months (Magistrates’ Court) → error; youth detention already being served counts only to the extent new detention is cumulated on it (terms are presumed concurrent: yjc.concurrency): its unexpired part + the part of the new detention cumulated on it > that maximum → error (app policy: the unexpired part); over the maximum only if the whole earlier term is counted instead → caution (flag.youth_detention_cap_across_occasions); new detention wholly concurrent with it adds nothing; new detention cumulated on it with the unexpired part unknown → caution (ask the user); aggregate detention with fewer than two offences, above the notional separate total, or without the announcement of decision, reasons and effect → error; pre-detention custody not declared (days) and no order otherwise → error; an order otherwise without a stated reason → caution (app policy, by analogy with the adult good-reason rule, 8.6.1); imprisonment on one charge above the YJC maximum with a YJC on another → caution.
logic: if type in ('yjc','yrc'): assert 15 <= age_sentence < 21 (yjc) or age_sentence < 15 (yrc); assert psr and finding; if syo in (A, B_with_prior): assert exceptional_circumstances; if syo is None: caution; cap = 48 (SC/CC) or 24 (MC); assert yd_effective_now <= cap (concurrent terms not added); c_yd = Σ months of new detention cumulated on the detention being served (charges[].cumulation onto 'yd_current'); if c_yd: (caution if yd_current_unexpired is None, else assert yd_current_unexpired + c_yd <= cap (app policy)); if c_yd and yd_current_whole_term + c_yd > cap: caution (flag.youth_detention_cap_across_occasions); if yd_aggregate: assert n >= 2 and months <= notional and announced; assert psd_days is not None or otherwise_ordered; if otherwise_ordered and not otherwise_reason: caution

title: Adjourned undertakings, DATOs, RTOs, CSTOs, court assessment orders, suspended and indefinite sentences: limits
statement: An adjourned undertaking may be up to five years and needs the offender’s agreement. A DATO is made only by the Drug Court within the listed eligibility and exclusions, with a custodial part of no more than 2 years (Magistrates’ Court) or 4 years (County Court) and no non-parole period. An RTO is limited to five years, to eligible offences and to eligible offenders, and RTOs cannot be cumulated. A CSTO must not exceed the imprisonment otherwise imposed and needs a non-parole period. Suspended sentences are abolished for offences after the listed dates. An indefinite sentence is exceptional and requires a high degree of probability of serious danger.
test: Adjourned undertaking: > 60 months → error; the offender’s agreement not recorded (fact or stated assumption) → caution. DATO: court not a Drug Court Division → error; the assessment report ordered and received, and the offender’s written consent, not recorded (fact or stated assumption) → caution; no guilty plea to an imprisonable charge → error; custodial part > 24 months (Drug Court MC) / 48 months (Drug Court CC), or an npp on it → error; offender currently on a DATO, on parole or subject to a higher-court sentence → error; excluded offence (sexual offences: the user states the offence is a schedule 1 sexual offence → error; otherwise a 24.1.1, 24.1.2 or 24.1.4 offence → caution, unresolved (24.5: “a sexual offence”, whose footnote cites s 18Z(1)(a)(i), the schedule 1 provision; app policy: no DATO is proposed for one unless the user states it is not a schedule 1 sexual offence), and a 24.1.3 (child abuse material) or 24.1.5 (sexual servitude) offence of unknown status → caution (flag.dato_sexual_offence_scope); covered by ss 10–10AE, i.e. the gross violence, protected officials, supervision-order, aggravated home invasion / carjacking and driving-against-protected-workers minimum groups) → error; actual bodily harm → error, except in the Magistrates’ Drug Court where the harm was minor (pass) or its nature is unknown (caution); custodial part lengthened to allow treatment → error (critic: audit.parsimony_and_cco). RTO: an RTO charge the user states is not an eligible offence → error; a charge outside the printed categories → caution, ask the user to confirm eligibility (flag.rto_serious_offence_list); total RTO months > 60 (no cumulation) → error; intellectual disability and the DHS Secretary’s specification not recorded → caution. CSTO: no notional imprisonment stated → error; CSTO months > notional months → error; no npp → error, except caution where the notional term is under 24 months or the reasoning states why an npp is inappropriate (8.3, applied “as if” imprisonment: flag.csto_npp_short_terms); an npp fixed where the notional term is under 12 months → caution (15.4.2 v 8.3.1: flag.csto_npp_short_terms); imprisonment with a direction that it be served in a mental health service → error. Court assessment order: offender in custody pending sentence → error. Suspended sentence: offence committed after the abolition date for the court and offence class → error; on that date → caution (flag.suspended_on_date); before it → caution (the regime is not in the Manual; the app does not propose one). Indefinite sentence: proposed other than for an adult convicted of a serious offence in the Supreme or County Court, without first excluding a Court Secure Treatment Order, without the serious-danger finding to a high degree of probability (prosecution burden) and the mandatory considerations, or with a non-parole period instead of a nominal sentence → error. The app never presents an indefinite sentence as the expected outcome. Contempt (the 29.1.3 rows): the Sentencing Act applies only in part, the Supreme Court may impose a suspended sentence, and coercive punishment of indeterminate length may be appropriate for refusal to give evidence (VSM 29.5.2) — so a suspended or indeterminate committal for contempt → caution citing flag.contempt_sentencing_act_and_orders, never error; the suspended-sentence and indefinite-sentence limbs above do not apply to contempt.
logic: if type=='adjourned_undertaking': assert months <= 60; if type=='dato': caution if not (assessment_report_received and written_consent); assert court in (DrugCourt-MC, DrugCourt-CC) and guilty_plea_imprisonable and custodial_months <= (24 if DrugCourt-MC else 48) and not npp and not current_dato and not on_parole and not higher_court_sentence and not excluded (sexual: classes.schedule_1_sexual is True → error; section in (24.1.1, 24.1.2, 24.1.4) and not True → caution (app policy: not proposed unless classes.schedule_1_sexual is False); 24.1.3/24.1.5 and None → caution; abh: pass if DrugCourt-MC and minor; caution if unknown); if type=='rto': assert total_months <= 60 and not any(user_states_ineligible); caution if any(not in_printed_category) (flag.rto_serious_offence_list); if type=='csto': assert notional and months <= notional and (npp or (notional < 24 or npp_inappropriate_reason): caution); if npp and notional < 12: caution (flag.csto_npp_short_terms); if type=='suspended': error if offence_date > abolition_date(court, class); caution otherwise; if offence in contempt rows (29.1.3) and type in ('suspended', 'indefinite'): caution (flag.contempt_sentencing_act_and_orders) instead of error

title: Mandatory ancillary orders: licence cancellation and disqualification; alcohol exclusion orders
statement: Licence disqualification is mandatory for serious motor vehicle offences (16.1 “found guilty or convicted”; 2.4.3 “found guilty and convicted”: flag.licence_guilty_or_convicted), and on conviction for dangerous or negligent driving while pursued by police and for stealing a motor vehicle, with statutory minimum periods; the form of the order depends on the licence held. AEO: conviction recorded ∧ relevant offence ∧ intoxicated by liquor ∧ intoxication significantly contributed (balance of probabilities) ∧ no previous AEO for the offence → the output must list an AEO (two years) → error if missing; any element unknown → caution, not error. Discretionary orders are listed as available, not as made, and only where their gate conditions (anc.*, order.licence.discretionary) are met in that court; unknown conditions → listed conditionally.
logic: for c in charges: g = serious_mv_group(c, facts); if g: assert licence_order and licence_order.months >= MIN[g] and licence_order.form == form(licence_status); if g and not c.conviction_recorded: caution; if c.offence == s319AA and c.conviction_recorded: assert licence_order.months >= 12; if vehicle_theft(c) and c.conviction_recorded: assert licence_order; if c.offence == RSA s61(3): prior = c.previous_s61_3_offence; m = (96 if c.conviction_recorded else 48) if prior else (48 if c.conviction_recorded else 24); assert licence_order.months >= m and licence_order.form == form(licence_status) (no Victorian licence held: caution); if prior is None: caution; aeo_required = conviction and relevant and intoxicated_by_liquor and contributed and not previous_aeo; if aeo_required: assert aeo; if any element is None: caution

title: Displacing presumptive cumulation for prison offences, escape and parole offending; youth centre escape or damage
statement: For a prison offence, escape, breach of parole or offending while on parole, a court must find exceptional circumstances before displacing the prima facie cumulation of the new sentence on the previous sentence. Youth detention for escaping from or damaging a youth justice or residential centre must be cumulative on other detention unless the court orders otherwise and gives reasons.
test: If a charge is a prison offence, escape, breach of parole or an offence committed while on parole and its sentence is made concurrent with the previous (uncompleted) sentence → error unless the reasoning finds exceptional circumstances and states them. Parole offending: the s 16(3B) default applies only where parole was cancelled before sentencing; where parole has not been cancelled at the time of sentencing no s 16(3B) order (cumulation or concurrency) may be made → no error; caution (flag.parole_not_cancelled_at_sentence); cancellation unknown → unresolved, ask the user. (Concurrency among the new charges themselves is not this test: cumulation may be ordered between offences committed on parole independently of the parole sentence.) If youth detention for escape from or damage to a youth justice or youth residential centre is made concurrent with other detention → error unless reasons for concurrency are stated. Parole from a life sentence: re-offending on life parole is itself an exceptional circumstance warranting a concurrent term (3.3.3), and no term may be cumulated on the life term (cum.life_parole) — a concurrent order → pass without a separate finding.

title: Instinctive synthesis, not two-tier sentencing or quantified discounts
statement: Sentence is reached by identifying all relevant factors, discussing their significance and making a value judgment. Two-tier sentencing — a benchmark taken from one consideration followed by proportional additions or deductions for others — is error, as is synthesising in stages; but the prohibition is not on sequential reasoning, or even arithmetic deductions, in certain cases. Quantifying a discount is inconsistent with the synthesis, except where the Act requires the plea discount to be identified (s 6AAA). For cooperation, the undiscounted sentence need not be stated, and stating it is undesirable save in the simplest cases. Classing offending as “low”, “mid-range” or “high” risks reading current practices for that class without the circumstances of the case.
test: (1) The reasoning starts from a figure — a benchmark, the maximum, a median, a co-offender’s sentence, the standard sentence, or a range attached to a category — and then adds or deducts amounts or percentages for factors → error. (2) A number or percentage is attached to an individual aggravating or mitigating factor (other than the s 6AAA notional sentence, and a stated but-for-cooperation sentence, which limb (4) governs) → error. (3) Arithmetic that belongs to a lawful step is not two-tier: deducting pre-sentence detention, summing cumulated terms, the s 6AAA comparison, combination-sentence and aggregate calculations → pass. (4) The sentence that would have been imposed but for cooperation is stated other than in a simple case → caution. (5) A category label (“low”, “mid-range”, “high”) is used to select a range from comparables or statistics → caution. Pass if the factors are weighed together and a sentence then stated, with the s 6AAA figure stated separately.
message: The reasoning uses a stepwise or arithmetic approach the Manual describes as error, or a category label that limits the synthesis (VSM 2.1, 2.1.1, 7.3.3.1).

refs.q: The instinctive synthesis is where a court identifies all relevant factors, discusses their significance, and at the end of the process makes a value judgment as to the appropriate sentence given its synthesis of the factors. It is a discretionary exercise, and weight cannot be allocated to the factors in advance. The correct weight is determined by the circumstances and there is no single correct sentence.

title: Sentencing statistics and medians are not used as the answer
statement: Statistics are a yardstick only: they do not identify the range, cannot substitute for the synthesis and do not by themselves establish a sentencing practice; a median is an accidental or contingent statistic. Selecting a median and placing the offending above or below it risks an improper two-stage approach. Used correctly, statistics may help to check whether a sentence accords with current sentencing practices.

title: Comparable cases (including retrieved case summaries) used as yardsticks only
statement: Current sentencing practices must be considered but are one factor among many. Comparable cases indicate a range that does not set the outer limits; a few cases do not define a range; detailed analysis to find the “right” sentence is wrong; comparisons are of limited use for widely varying offences. Strict regard must be had to the offence under consideration; a range that appears contrary to principle should not be followed; cases with idiosyncratic features are unlikely to be useful comparators; cases predating an appellate statement that practices were inadequate need great caution, as do cases decided under a lower maximum (an increase signals that existing sentences were insufficient); Victorian courts do not often give substantial weight to other States’ practices. For historic offences, caution is called for where the maximum is now higher, and equal justice may require regard to historical practices — but an offender whose own conduct prevented contemporaneous sentencing may not be able to rely on them (24.1.8.1). Where a party relies on a strikingly similar case, the court must ordinarily explain how it informed the discretion.
test: For each retrieved or user-supplied case relied on: (1) the reasoning states how it is relevantly similar or instructively different → caution if not; (2) cases are averaged or interpolated, a handful treated as a binding range, or the estimate derived by matching one case → caution (and error under audit.instinctive_synthesis_not_two_tier if it becomes a starting figure); (3) the case is for a different offence, from another State, decided before an appellate call for change, or decided under a lower maximum than now applies → caution, flag it; (4) a range that appears contrary to principle, or a case with idiosyncratic features, is followed → caution; (5) historic offending: the reasoning does not apply 5.2.9.2.1 (and, for sexual offences, 24.1.8.1) → caution; (6) a case the user relies on as strikingly similar: the reasoning does not say how it informed the estimate → caution.
message: Treat the similar cases as yardsticks, not as setting the sentence (VSM 5.1.3, 5.2.9.1–5.2.9.3.1, 24.1.8.1).

title: Standard sentence taken into account as a guidepost; relationship stated; only scheme sentences as practice
statement: The standard sentence is a legislative guidepost like the maximum. The key requirement is that it be taken into account as a relevant sentencing factor, but it must not be given too much weight; the court does not start from it and work up or down, and must state how the sentence relates to it by identifying the facts, matters and circumstances bearing on its judgment, without classifying the offence against a hypothetical mid-range instance. For a standard sentence offence a court may only consider sentences previously imposed under the scheme as current practice, though principles established in earlier cases remain usable.
test: Only for a charge within the scheme (sso.scope: offence date, offender age, jurisdiction): (1) the reasoning begins from the standard sentence and adjusts → error; (2) it labels the offending “below/above mid-range” as the reason → error; (3) it does not state how the sentence relates to the standard sentence → error; (4) the standard sentence is not taken into account at all → error; (5) it is treated as decisive or given excessive weight → caution; (6) sentences imposed before the scheme are used as current sentencing practice → error (drawing principles from those cases → pass).
message: Take the standard sentence into account and explain how the sentence relates to it, without treating it as a starting point (VSM 9.2).

title: No reliance on adverse matters the user has not supplied; assumptions surfaced
statement: A party must be made aware of any information on which an adverse determination may be based and given an opportunity to respond; a court may not sentence on a fact it considers important (e.g. prevalence, whether a factor aggravates) without identifying it, nor on material not before it. Where the facts of the offence are disputed, no adverse inference may be drawn from the offender’s failure to give evidence on the plea except in rare and exceptional circumstances. (For a fine, an adverse inference may be drawn if the offender declines to disclose their financial circumstances.)
test: (1) List every matter adverse to the offender that the reasoning relies on; any that is not in the user’s facts and not expressly labelled as an assumption the user must confirm → error. (2) On disputed facts of the offence, an adverse inference is drawn from the offender not giving evidence on the plea, without identifying rare and exceptional circumstances → error. (3) An inference about means from a refusal to disclose financial circumstances when fixing a fine → pass.
message: The estimate relies on adverse matters not in the facts provided; these are listed as assumptions (VSM 2.2.2.2, 2.2.2.2.1).

refs.q: It is the fundamental requirement that a party who is potentially subject to ‘an adverse determination on the basis of any information, whatever its source, must be made aware’ of the information and given an opportunity to respond.

title: An element of the offence is not counted as aggravating or mitigating
statement: In categorising facts as aggravating or mitigating, a factor that is an element of the offence cannot be counted; conduct exceeding the minimum needed for an element can show a more serious example.
test: Compare each listed aggravating and mitigating factor with the elements of the offence charged (e.g. the weapon in armed robbery, the injury in a causing-injury offence, the child’s age in a child sexual offence). (1) An element is listed as aggravating, unless the reasoning explains the excess over the minimum the element requires → error. (2) An element is counted as mitigating → error. (3) Where carrying a weapon is an element of a violent theft offence, the nature of the weapon, its potential to cause harm and the manner of its use may still be considered; for aggravated carjacking the use of a weapon in aid of the carjacking will almost always heighten gravity although it is the qualifying circumstance (VSM 27.2.2.3) → pass where the reasoning addresses how the weapon was used. (4) Firearm possession offences in which prohibited-person or firearm prohibition order status is an element (s 5(1), s 5(2), s 5AB(2), s 5AB(3), s 112B): the status counted again as aggravating → caution (flag.firearm_status_priors_aggravation), not error; the reason for the prohibition may inform gravity (VSM 33.2.1.1).
message: An element of the offence appears to be counted as aggravating or mitigating (VSM 5.2.8).

title: Uncharged conduct: aggravating only within the De Simoni limits
statement: The circumstances of an offence are not confined to its elements: uncharged or discreditable conduct may be treated as aggravating. But it may not be taken into account where it constitutes an aggravated version of the offending or should have been alleged as a separate charge entirely, and uncharged acts cannot aggravate where they warrant conviction for a more serious offence; the court sentences only for the offence of which the person is convicted or to which they plead. The Manual’s permitted examples include an uncharged injury when sentencing for recklessly exposing an emergency worker to risk (no separate injury charge) and offending while on conditional liberty or in breach of court orders; uncharged offending may also be mentioned as part of the narrative. The line is fine and fact-dependent.
test: For each surrounding fact used to increase seriousness ask whether it (a) is an aggravated version of the charged offence, (b) should have been alleged as a separate charge entirely, (c) would warrant conviction for a more serious offence, or (d) is itself separately charged and sentenced (then audit.double_punishment). (1) Yes to (a), (b) or (c) and it is used to increase the sentence → error. (2) Conduct of the kinds the Manual permits (e.g. an uncharged injury on a reckless-exposure charge with no separate injury charge; offending on conditional liberty or in breach of a court order) → pass; for the conditional-liberty and enlisting-others-to-lie examples show the Manual’s contrary-authority note (flag.contrary_authority_signals_5_6) → caution. (3) Borderline cases (contemporaneity; disparity in seriousness between the charged and uncharged conduct) → caution. (4) Uncharged conduct mentioned as narrative without being used to increase the sentence → pass. (5) Aggravated burglary or home invasion: an uncharged loaded firearm carried during the entry, relied on only for what it shows about the charged entry (premeditation, intention at entry, increased danger) → caution citing flag.uncharged_firearm_clark (VSM 27.2.2.2), not error.
message: The reasoning may punish uncharged or more serious conduct (VSM 2.2.2.2.1, 2.3.1.2, 2.4.3, 5.2.8.5).

refs.q: Uncharged conduct or discreditable conduct may be treated as an aggravating feature of the offence, and as an indicator of increased moral culpability. But where the uncharged conduct constitutes an aggravated version of the offending or should have been alleged as a separate charge entirely, a court may not take it into account. Uncharged acts cannot be taken as aggravating factors where they warrant conviction for a more serious offence.

title: No double punishment or double counting (separate harms excepted)
statement: A person must not be punished twice for the same criminal conduct or for common elements; a wholly subsumed offence is not separately sentenced even concurrently; conduct separately sentenced cannot also aggravate another charge; breach of trust cannot both aggravate and diminish good character. But where a single act reflects separate harms, particularly against different people, each may be punished separately even when linked by time and place, and an appropriate measure of cumulation may be called for (e.g. culpable driving causing several deaths or serious injuries). The Manual describes the area as complex and ambiguous, with varied outcomes.
test: (1) Clear cases → error: a wholly subsumed offence separately sentenced; the identical act or element used to increase two sentences without concurrency reflecting the overlap; conduct separately sentenced also used to aggravate another charge; one factor used twice (e.g. breach of trust as aggravating and to reduce good character). (2) Separate harms from a single act, especially to different victims, punished separately or cumulated → pass. (3) Borderline overlap (partly shared conduct; whether the harms are separate is unclear) → caution.
message: The same conduct or factor appears to be punished twice (VSM 3.4, 3.4.4, 5.2.8.5, 6.3.1.1).

title: Mandatory and statutory considerations addressed (and only proper ones)
statement: All relevant factors must be identified and their significance discussed; where legislation directs that a matter be considered, it should be discussed, not merely recited. The maximum penalty and current sentencing practices are mandatory considerations, as is the standard sentence for a standard sentence offence. The s 5(2) matters include the nature and gravity of the offence, culpability and degree of responsibility, the circumstances of the victim, any injury, loss or damage resulting directly from the offending, the impact on any victim, a hatred or prejudice motive, personal circumstances, the plea and previous character. Family violence calls for denunciation and the surrounding behaviours must be considered; offence-specific guidance for the charged offence must be considered.
test: (1) The maximum penalty, current sentencing practices or — for a charge within the standard sentence scheme — the standard sentence is not addressed at all → error. (2) Each of the following not addressed where relevant → caution: the nature and gravity of the offence; culpability and degree of responsibility; the circumstances of the victim; any injury, loss or damage resulting directly from the offending; the impact on the victim; a hatred or prejudice motive (if any facts suggest it); personal circumstances; plea; previous character; each offence-guide item linked to the charged offence. (3) A statutory matter recited rather than discussed → caution.

title: Prior convictions, lack of remorse and a not guilty plea are not aggravating
statement: Prior criminality cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence or to doubly punish, but it may indicate moral culpability, persistent lawlessness or a propensity to commit particular crimes and so inhibit mitigation such as rehabilitation; subsequent convictions cannot increase the head sentence. Absence of remorse is not aggravating, but it may show a need for specific deterrence and, where it reveals a contemptuous attitude to the victim or the law, may bear on moral culpability and prospects for rehabilitation. A not guilty plea is never aggravating. Some offence chapters use looser language; those passages are flagged and the flags are shown with this check.
test: (1) Priors, subsequent convictions, lack of remorse, a not guilty plea or the conduct of the defence are labelled or weighed as aggravating circumstances, or used to lift the sentence above what the offence warrants → error. (2) Priors used to deny leniency, to weigh specific deterrence or community protection, or as showing moral culpability or persistent lawlessness that limits mitigation; lack of remorse used for specific deterrence or (where it shows contempt) culpability and rehabilitation prospects → pass. (3) Similar priors treated as part of the context when comparing co-offenders (30.3), or an offence chapter that lists one of these matters as aggravating → caution, with the relevant flag. (4) An OHS offence committed before 1 July 2005 by an offender previously convicted under the OHSA 1985: an additional penalty under OHSA 1985 s 53 is a statutory penalty the Manual describes for that case, so imposing it is not an error under this check, provided the prior convictions are omitted from the base penalty; priors counted both in the base penalty and in the s 53 additional penalty → error (no double counting, VSM 31.1.2).
message: Priors, lack of remorse or a not guilty plea are being treated as aggravating (VSM 6.3.1.2, 6.3.4.1, 7.1.2.1).

refs.q: Evidence of an offender’s bad character, i.e., their prior criminality, is also relevant to a court in exercising the sentencing discretion, but it cannot be used in aggravation to increase a sentence or to doubly punish an offender. Instead, it may indicate an offender’s moral culpability, persistent lawlessness or a propensity to commit particular crimes and so inhibit consideration of mitigatory factors such as rehabilitation.

title: Verdins applied only on cogent evidence, limb by limb
statement: Generally, Verdins need only be considered where the issue is clearly raised with a sufficient evidentiary basis; it is wrong to assume it applies because an impairment exists. Cogent evidence, normally expert evidence, must establish on the balance of probabilities that the principles are enlivened; the Manual also says expert evidence is required but not determinative, and the court decides whether and how each limb applies. Some connection between the impairment and the offending is required to moderate general deterrence or reduce culpability (a causal connection is not required). General deterrence should not be moderated where the impairment arose as a reaction to the discovery of the crimes or the prospect of imprisonment (that does not matter for the burden-of-imprisonment limbs). A self-induced impairment may reduce the mitigatory effect. A court may infer, without direct evidence, that a prisoner with a severe mental health condition would find prison more burdensome.
test: (1) The estimate moderates general deterrence, reduces culpability or treats prison as more burdensome because of an impairment the facts do not evidence → error; without such evidence the Verdins effect may be shown only as a conditional alternative (“if cogent, normally expert, evidence establishes …”; flag.verdins_expert_evidence_normally_vs_required). (2) Verdins is applied without naming the limb(s) and why each applies → error. (3) General deterrence moderated or culpability reduced without some connection to the offending → error (strict causation is not required: flag.verdins_connection_test). (4) General deterrence moderated where the impairment arose on discovery of the crimes or at the prospect of prison → error. (5) A self-induced impairment given full mitigatory effect without addressing 6.2.2.9 → caution. (6) The greater burden of imprisonment inferred for a severe condition shown by other evidence, without expert evidence → caution (a permitted inference, 6.2.2.6).
message: Mental impairment is relied on without the evidence or the limb-by-limb analysis Verdins requires (VSM 6.2.2.2, 6.2.2.4, 6.2.2.6, 6.2.2.9, 6.2.2.11).

refs.q: Generally, a court only needs to consider the Verdins principles in cases where the issue is clearly raised by counsel, and there is a sufficient evidentiary basis to do so.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: It is mechanistic, simplistic, and wrong to say that because an offender suffers from a mental impairment the Verdins principles apply. There has to be a careful and rigorous consideration of whether the evidence establishes that the offender’s mental capacity has been impaired and which of the circumstances identified in Verdins are applicable.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: There needs to be cogent evidence, normally in the form of expert evidence, establishing on the balance of the probabilities that the Verdins principles are enlivened. The evidence must establish that the impairment existed at the time of offending, sentence, or both, as well as its nature, extent, and effect on the offender or its likely effect on them in the future. Expert evidence also needs to be assessed against what is known about the circumstances of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: While expert evidence is required, it is not determinative, and it is ultimately for the court, not a psychiatrist or psychologist, to decide if and how the Verdins principles apply in a given case. It is wholly outside of a psychiatrist’s or psychologist’s expertise to express a view on whether one or more of the principles apply, and practitioners relying on expert reports should ensure they don’t contain impermissible opinions of that kind.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.11 – Consideration and evidence

refs.q: General deterrence may be moderated or eliminated if an offender suffers from an impairment at the time of offending, sentencing, or both. But Verdins does not automatically require that general deterrence be modified where a person’s mental functioning is impaired.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence

refs.q: Further, there must be an evidentiary basis to moderate general deterrence. It is not sufficient to find that an offender suffers from a mental impairment. There must be ‘proper and informed’ consideration of how the impairment materially diminished the offender’s capacity to reason appropriately about the wrongfulness of their conduct at the time of the offending, or how the offender’s condition might make full application of the principles of general deterrence repugnant to the humanitarian considerations that guide proper sentencing.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence

refs.q: It is also clear that general deterrence should not be moderated where the offender’s mental impairment arose as a reaction to the discovery of their crimes or the prospect of incarceration.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.4 – General deterrence

refs.q: While a causal connection is not required by Verdins to reduce the offender’s culpability (or to moderate or eliminate general and specific deterrence), some connection is still required. If the impairment existed at the time of the offending there must be a ‘realistic connection’ between the two, or the impairment must have ‘caused or contributed to’ or be ‘causally linked’ to the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.2 – Health > 6.2.2 – Mental impairment > 6.2.2.2 – Moral culpability

refs.q: The mitigatory effect of mental impairment may be reduced where the condition is self-induced, often by drug or alcohol use. The key issue is what the offender knew about the possible consequences of taking the relevant substance, what is required is foreknowledge that use of a substance ‘was likely to produce a delusional state’.

refs.q: In either case, it does not matter that an offender’s mental impairment arose because their crimes were discovered or due to the prospect of incarceration. If their condition is likely to be aggravated by the experience of imprisonment, a court may reduce the offender’s sentence. However, the weight to be given to these considerations always varies and does not displace consideration of the other sentencing purposes in the instinctive synthesis.

title: Intoxication, addiction and good character given only their proper weight
statement: Intoxication will rarely mitigate (only in exceptional circumstances) and may aggravate, particularly where the offender knew the likely consequences of ingestion. Addiction may bear on culpability and other purposes, but its weight is greatly diminished above street level, someone with repeated opportunities for reform should not expect to rely on it, and if the lack of an addiction is used to show the offender acted solely from greed it must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Good character is assessed apart from the current offending, carries reduced weight for offences commonly committed by people of otherwise good character, and in sentencing for a child sexual offence cannot be considered if the court is satisfied that it helped the offender commit the offence.
test: (1) Good character used in mitigation for a child sexual offence where the facts show it helped the offender commit the offence → error (where that is unclear, the finding is for the court → caution). (2) The current offending used to deny good character → error. (3) Lack of addiction used to infer greed without proof beyond reasonable doubt → error. (4) Intoxication treated as mitigating without exceptional circumstances, or not considered as possibly aggravating where the offender knew the likely consequences → caution. (5) Addiction given substantial weight for above-street-level trafficking or for an offender with repeated opportunities for reform → caution. (6) Good character given full weight where the offence is one commonly committed by people of good character or exploited respectability → caution.
message: Check the weight given to intoxication, addiction or good character (VSM 6.2.3, 6.2.4, 6.3.1.1).

refs.q: Intoxication – whether through alcohol or narcotic consumption – will rarely mitigate offending, and may even be an aggravating factor. For intoxication to reduce moral culpability, the circumstances will have to be ‘quite exceptional’. The key question is the degree of foreknowledge. If the offender knew of the likely consequences of drug ingestion their culpability is increased, and intoxication may be an aggravating factor. Where a long history of alcohol consumption has not revealed the slightest indication that an offender poses a risk of violence, this may mean the circumstances are sufficiently exceptional to be mitigating.

title: No differential sentencing on race, ethnicity, culture, religion or gender in themselves; Bugmy applied correctly
statement: Ethnicity, culture and race are not in themselves bases for differential sentencing, though associated considerations may be, depending on their connection with the offence; a cultural norm must be established by evidence relevant to the offender and cannot give rise to a different range of sentences for a group; treating Aboriginal offenders as generally less culpable is racial stereotyping, though deprivation mitigates to the same extent for all; there can be no difference in sentencing based solely on gender, though closely associated factors such as pregnancy may be considered; general deterrence must not be used to target an ethnic community. Religious practices likely to make an offender a target in prison may be taken into account. It is an error to require an offender to demonstrate “significant childhood deprivation”; at some point mitigation for disadvantage must yield to serious violent offending and community protection, particularly in domestic violence.
test: (1) The sentence is adjusted by reference to race, ethnicity, culture, religion or gender as such, rather than a specific connected circumstance supported by the facts (deprivation, a proved cultural factor bearing on the offence, pregnancy, religious practices making the offender a target in prison) → error. (2) General deterrence is directed at an ethnic community → error. (3) A cultural norm is acted on without evidence relevant to the offender, or used to set a different range for a group → error. (4) Bugmy mitigation refused because deprivation is not shown to be “significant” or “profound” → error; any other threshold label (e.g. “extreme”) applied to the general expression → caution (flag.bugmy_degree_of_deprivation). (5) Deprivation given full weight for serious violent or domestic violence offending without considering that mitigation may yield → caution.
message: The reasoning appears to rely on a personal attribute in itself, or misapplies Bugmy (VSM 4.2.1, 6.1.2, 6.1.3, 6.3.3.1, 7.6.2.5).
