refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.5 – Nationality and religion

refs.q: However, it is an error to require the offender to demonstrate ‘significant childhood deprivation’. There is no requirement that the deprivation be “profound”.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

refs.q: While disadvantage will always remain relevant, at some point mitigation must yield in the face of serious violent offending and the need for community protection. This is particularly so in cases of domestic violence; childhood disadvantage cannot mitigate a sentence, ‘such that victims of domestic violence… are treated as less worthy of protection or that the crimes against them warrant less denunciation’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.3 – Personal history and circumstances > 6.3.3.1 – Childhood

title: Plea: utilitarian value, timing, remorse and application of the discount
statement: The Act requires the court to consider whether the offender pleaded guilty and at what stage. In all but exceptional cases the utilitarian value of a plea must be acknowledged by a reduction; the strength of the Crown case has no bearing on that value; pleading guilty to some charges while contesting others does not diminish the weight of the plea. Timing is assessed from when a plea was first reasonably open; early pleas ordinarily attract a substantial discount, late ones generally less. A further reduction for remorse requires proper evidence of genuine penitence, and post-offence remorse may not be rejected merely because remorse was lacking at the time of the offending. The discount is applied to the head sentence and then the non-parole period. There are competing authorities on a discount in the worst category, and the pandemic augmentation was noted to have subsided by the end of 2023.
test: (1) A guilty plea given no reduction without identifying exceptional circumstances → error. (2) The strength of the Crown case used to reduce the utilitarian value → error. (3) Post-offence remorse rejected because it is inconsistent with a lack of remorse at the time of the offending → error. (4) Timing characterised without reference to when a plea was first reasonably open, or a plea’s weight reduced because other charges were contested → caution. (5) Remorse inferred from the plea alone without evidence, or the discount not reflected in the non-parole period → caution. (6) A discount refused or allowed for worst-category offending (flag.worst_category_plea_competing_authority), a pandemic augmentation (flag.covid_custody_currency), or timing affected by forensic prejudice (flag.plea_timing_forensic_prejudice) → caution.
message: Check the treatment of the plea and remorse (VSM 4.3, 6.3.4.1, 7.1.1–7.1.3.3).

refs.q: The Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) (‘the Act’) requires a court to consider whether the offender pleaded guilty and at what stage in the proceedings any plea or intention to plead occurred.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

refs.q: Every plea of guilty must be considered in sentencing. But the weight to be given it depends upon the circumstances of each case and should be the result of ‘specific and sound’ consideration. A plea does not always need to result in a sentencing discount, nor is the court bound to accept a Crown concession that a guilty plea should reduce the sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight

refs.q: In all but exceptional cases, the utilitarian value of a plea must be acknowledged by a reduction in the sentence imposed. This recognises the objective benefit to the community regardless of whether the plea is accompanied by any evidence of remorse or contrition. Even a plea motivated by self-interest has a utilitarian benefit.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

refs.q: The strength of the Crown case will have no bearing on the assessment of (and reward for) the utilitarian value of a guilty plea because it does not bear upon the objective benefits of the plea. But the length and complexity of any trial that has been rendered unnecessary by the guilty plea is relevant to the assessment of the utilitarian benefit.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

refs.q: When an accused pleads guilty to some charges but contests others, this does not diminish the weight to be attached to the utilitarian benefit of the pleas of guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.1 – Utilitarian benefit

refs.q: A plea given early and unconditionally should ordinarily attract a substantial sentencing discount. A plea made at the earliest opportunity that evidences genuine remorse and prospects of rehabilitation, which saves the State a trial and witnesses trauma and inconvenience, normally justifies a high discount. An early plea that does nothing but save the costs of a trial usually still attracts a significant discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

refs.q: A late plea attracts a discount, but it will generally be of lower value. How the timing of a guilty plea is characterised depends on the facts of the case and involves establishing the time it could first be said it was reasonably open to the offender to plead guilty.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.2 – Weight > 7.1.2.3 – Timing

refs.q: An offender who wants to rely on remorse in mitigation must ‘satisfy the court there is genuine penitence and contrition and a desire to atone’. This must be established on proper evidence and a court should be cautious before accepting that an offender’s guilty plea indicates remorse warranting more than a utilitarian discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 6 – Circumstances of the offender > 6.3 – Actions and behaviour > 6.3.4 – Remorse and restitution > 6.3.4.1 – Remorse

refs.q: Remorse is measured by post-conduct action and while a court is not bound to accept it, it is error not to do so because it was inconsistent with a lack of remorse at the time of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: Where a sentence of imprisonment is imposed, the discount is first applied to the head sentence as the prisoner must, hypothetically, serve every day of that sentence. Next, the discount is applied to the non-parole period. The plea may even incur an additional discount at this stage if it also evidences rehabilitative prospects.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.1 – Imprisonment

refs.q: There are competing authorities on the question of whether an offender pleading guilty to an offence in the ‘worst category’ of offending should be entitled to a discount for their plea.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.3 – Application of discount > 7.1.3.3 – Gravity of offending

refs.q: It has been noted, however, that as at the end of 2023 the effects of the pandemic upon the criminal justice system in Victoria have subsided.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.1 – Guilty plea > 7.1.1 – Benefits

title: Cooperation with authorities: no tariff; nature of the assistance explained
statement: There is no mathematical process or tariff for a cooperation discount: it rises or falls with objective and subjective factors and the nature of the assistance (the highest levels of cooperation have attracted 50% to 66%). The announcement of a less severe sentence for cooperation is checked by audit.cooperation_statement; the undiscounted sentence need not be stated and stating it is undesirable save in the simplest cases. Reasons may need a restricted and a public version.
test: (1) A fixed percentage applied as a rule or tariff → error. (2) Cooperation relied on without identifying the nature of the assistance and why it warrants the reduction → caution. (3) The undiscounted sentence stated other than in a simple case → caution. (4) Remind the user that published reasons may need to omit or veil the cooperation → caution.
message: Cooperation must be reflected without a tariff (VSM 7.3.2, 7.3.2.5, 7.3.3.1).

refs.q: The discount to be applied will rise or fall according to both objective and subjective factors. The lowest level of cooperation is making admissions and entering a plea of guilty. At higher levels, cooperation may involve implicating co-offenders or providing other information of assistance to authorities and giving evidence in criminal proceedings. The highest-level discount is reserved for so-called ‘true informers’, who assist authorities proactively, acting as ‘undercover’ agents to provide information and evidence, commonly at greatly increased personal risk.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount

refs.q: Many factors are relevant to the exercise of the discretion in these circumstances and there is no mathematical or mechanical process for fixing the value of the cooperation discount. The discount is determined according to a range of factors, including — but not limited to — the nature and extent of the cooperation, any willingness to give evidence against co-offenders, and any danger flowing from the cooperation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.1 – No ‘standard’ discount

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has said that the highest level of co-operation could attract discounts of 50% to 66% for a ‘true informer’. However there is no ‘tariff’ or standard discount. And the Court has emphasised the need to assess each discount for cooperation in context and to avoid approaching the task in a mathematical way.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.1 – No ‘standard’ discount

refs.q: However, the quantum of the sentence that the court would have imposed except for the undertaking does not have to be stated. The court may state the sentence that would have been imposed, but it is undesirable to do so except in the simplest cases that have a small number of relevant considerations.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.3 – State v Commonwealth scheme > 7.3.3.1 – Identification of discount

refs.q: • one that fully explains how the offender’s cooperation informed its exercise of the sentencing discretion; and • a second version, which may identify the offender by a pseudonym, that is either silent regarding the cooperation or makes only a ‘veiled reference’ to it.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.5 – Reporting cooperation

refs.q: The first version is restricted and is published only to the parties, the second is made publicly available.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.3 – Co-operation with the authorities > 7.3.2 – Applying the discount > 7.3.2.5 – Reporting cooperation

title: Delay and hardship: evidence and thresholds
statement: Delay is not an automatic discount. It has two limbs (unfairness to the offender; rehabilitation during the delay); the offender must provide some evidence for the limb relied on, though in some cases anxiety may be accepted without supporting evidence; it bears on both head sentence and non-parole period. Delay attributable to the offender carries less significance, and in sexual abuse prosecutions the accused often cannot rely on it. Hardship to the offender needs no exceptionality. Hardship to family or third parties is not normally mitigating; for Victorian offences the Manual records an earlier “exceptional” threshold and states that it now appears the hardship must rise above that commonly suffered by prisoners’ families and be so significant that it will weigh heavily — generally for an especially vulnerable dependant, on cogent evidence.
test: (1) Delay treated as automatically mitigating, or relied on without any evidence of the limb used (save anxiety the court may accept from the delay’s length and cause) → caution. (2) Delay attributable to the offender given full weight, or delay in a sexual abuse prosecution relied on without considering 7.5.2 → caution. (3) Third-party hardship mitigates without cogent evidence, or for hardship of the kind commonly suffered by prisoners’ families → error. (4) Which formulation of the third-party threshold governs (“exceptional” or “weigh heavily”) → caution (flag.third_party_hardship_exceptionality).
message: Check the basis for mitigation for delay or hardship (VSM 7.5–7.5.3.1, 7.6, 7.6.4).

refs.q: Significant delay between the time an offender is interviewed by police and the time charges are laid, as well as delay between the laying of charges and trial, can be a powerful mitigating factor. However, delay in itself creates no automatic right to a sentencing discount. The most that can be said is that where the prosecution unduly delays bringing the matter to court there is much more likely to be a discount.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay

refs.q: There are two limbs to delay as a mitigating factor. The first concerns unfairness to the offender in that a charge (or its prospect) was ‘hanging over’ their head and caused them anxiety (‘unfairness limb’). These effects are not eliminated by the offender’s failure to confess to undisclosed offences during the period of delay.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay

refs.q: Where an offender relies on either limb of delay, they must provide some evidence to support the submission.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.1 – Evidence of delay

refs.q: But there may also be cases where depending on the duration of the delay, its cause, and other circumstances, a court might accept that the delay caused anxiety to the offender without the need for supporting evidence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.1 – Evidence of delay

refs.q: Where delay is a relevant sentencing factor, it will be relevant to both head sentence and non-parole period. It is not an application of the totality principle for a sentence to be reduced because of the strain that an offender experiences by having a matter hanging over their head.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.5 – Form of impact on mitigation

refs.q: Where the crime being prosecuted is sexual abuse, the accused is often not able to rely upon delay in mitigation because delay in the detection or complaint of such abuse is a common consequence of the nature of the offending.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.2 – ‘Undue’ delay

refs.q: Where delay can be positively attributed to the offender, courts will give less significance to delay, even to the point of giving less credit for rehabilitation established during that period.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.5 – Delay > 7.5.3 – Responsibility for delay > 7.5.3.1 – Offender’s responsibility for delay

refs.q: Limbs one and three do not require the offender to establish any ‘exceptional’ hardship to mitigate sentence. The second limb, hardship to the family (or other associates) of the offender, demands that the offender establish exceptional circumstances before it will go to mitigating sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction

refs.q: Hardship to a third party as a consequence of imprisonment is not normally a mitigating circumstance. But a court has discretion to mitigate sentence when that sentence causes hardship to a third-party and it is satisfied there are exceptional circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: For Victorian offences, the Court of Appeal has previously said that hardship to third parties is only relevant in mitigation where it is ‘highly exceptional’ or ‘the exceptional case where the plea for mercy is seen as irresistible’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: It appears now that for Victorian offences, the circumstances must be such that they rise above the general and sometimes tragic hardship commonly suffered by the families of imprisoned offenders; they must be ‘so significant that they will weigh heavily in the sentencing calculus’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: This consideration will generally only arise where the third party is an especially vulnerable dependent of the offender, or where there are a number of vulnerable dependents.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

refs.q: Moreover, there must be cogent evidence that the offender’s imprisonment would expose the family member or third party to this hardship. This may also be established by a combination of lesser hardships to multiple family members. These cases will be rare. Whether or not, in any particular case, family hardship is sufficient to be significantly mitigating is a question of fact and degree.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.4 – Hardship to third parties/family

title: Prevalence used only with a disclosed basis and procedural fairness
statement: Prevalence is neither a circumstance of the offence nor of the offender; the better view is that reliance on it requires the court to disclose its source and give the parties an opportunity to address it, and a court may not sentence on a fact it considers important, such as prevalence, without first identifying it. Its principles are engaged only if it is used to aggravate. The evidentiary foundation remains unresolved, and recent cases focus on the content of the offending rather than a locality or ethnic community.
test: (1) The sentence is increased for prevalence without a stated, disclosed source, or without flagging that the parties must be given an opportunity to address it → error. (2) Prevalence based on a locality or an ethnic community → caution (and see audit.protected_attributes). (3) Whether the material relied on suffices to establish prevalence → caution (flag.prevalence_evidentiary_foundation; cite the 7.4.1 footnote with flag.ibid_1551_prevalence_attribution).
message: Prevalence is relied on without a disclosed basis (VSM 2.2.2.2.1, 7.4, 7.4.1, 7.4.2).

refs.q: Prevalence is neither a circumstance of the offence nor a circumstance of the offender; but rather is ‘a circumstance of other offences’. When and how prevalence can be invoked as a sentencing consideration has to be navigated carefully.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence

refs.q: Prevalence is not ‘a sentencing fact’ in the Storey sense and so does not need to be proved beyond reasonable doubt. All that is required is that a court should be sure that an offence is prevalent before weighting the instinctive synthesis in favour of general deterrence and giving less weight to mitigatory factors. But even if the court is certain that an offence is prevalent or locally prevalent, an increased sentence is not inevitable. There may be countervailing factors of greater significance.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: However, the better view is now that any reliance on prevalence as a sentencing factor demands the court afford the parties procedural fairness on the issue and disclose the source of the reasoning.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: While a judge may observe that an offence is common, or even prevalent, the principles applicable to ‘prevalence’ will not be invoked unless the court uses that consideration to aggravate the offence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.1 – Issues in relying on prevalence

refs.q: In the past, courts have sometimes found prevalence relevant to a particular locality or ethnic community. However, more recent cases focus on the content of the offending itself.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.4 – Prevalence > 7.4.2 – Nature of prevalence

refs.q: A court may not sentence an offender based on a fact it considers important — such as whether an offence is prevalent, or whether a factor is mitigating or aggravating — without first identifying the question and providing the parties with an opportunity to address the point.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.2 – The sentencing hearing > 2.2.2 – Judicial duties > 2.2.2.2 – Procedural fairness > 2.2.2.2.1 – Notice

title: The sentencing purposes identified and weighed (general deterrence not overwhelming; youth; impairment; protection)
statement: The s 5(1) purposes overlap, and which purpose, if any, is paramount depends on all the circumstances and is discretionary. General deterrence plays a role in almost every case but must not cause injustice by overwhelming the other purposes; it has minimal relevance when sentencing a child, and for youthful offenders rehabilitation is usually far more important. A disproportionate sentence may not be imposed to extend the protection of the community save under the statutory regimes; before imposing one the court must be satisfied the offender will remain a danger beyond the proportionate term and give reasons, and the serious-offender power should be exercised rarely.
test: (1) General deterrence relied on heavily for a child → error, unless the reasoning finds that punishment beyond what the CYFA (or s 32(3)(b)) allows, or adult custody, is necessary — then → caution (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges); general deterrence relied on without considering youth or impairment where raised → error. (2) Protection of the community used to exceed a proportionate sentence outside the statutory regimes → error. (3) Under a statutory regime, a disproportionate term proposed without satisfaction of continuing danger beyond the proportionate term and reasons → error. (4) The purposes engaged are not identified and weighed → caution (naming a paramount purpose is not required).
message: Check how the sentencing purposes were weighed (VSM 4, 4.2.1, 4.4, 9.3).

refs.q: More than one purpose may be (and often is) furthered by a given sentence, and determining which purpose, if any, is paramount depends on all circumstances and is a discretionary matter for the sentencing court.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes

refs.q: So, a court must be careful to ensure that general deterrence is not permitted to cause injustice, by so overwhelming the other sentencing purposes that an individual sentence becomes disproportionately harsh when assessed against the degree of criminality of an offender’s conduct.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: General deterrence has minimal relevance when sentencing a child.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: For youthful offenders, rehabilitation is usually far more important than general deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: A sentence must be proportionate to the crime, and a disproportionate sentence may not be imposed to extend the period of protection of society from the risk of recidivism on the part of an offender.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: And before imposing a disproportionate term to further the community’s protection, the court must also be satisfied that the prisoner will remain a danger to the community beyond the period proportionality would indicate is an appropriate term and it must provide reasons for doing so.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.4 – Protection of the community

refs.q: The power to impose a disproportionate sentence is one that should be exercised rarely.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 9 – Statutory Schemes > 9.3 – Serious offenders

refs.q: If the court does impose a disproportionate sentence, then failure to explain its reasons for assessing an offender as likely to remain a risk to the community beyond a proportionate term may give rise to appealable error.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 9 – Statutory Schemes > 9.3 – Serious offenders

title: Executive action, registration and deportation consequences handled correctly
statement: The court must not consider the possibility that time in custody may be affected by executive action, and must assume every day of the head sentence may be served; but in fixing the non-parole period it may consider the possibility of parole, its rehabilitative potential and the offender’s suitability. It must not consider Sex Offenders Registration Act or Working With Children Act consequences, and it is error to lower a sentence artificially to avoid Migration Act consequences. An offender must not be denied parole eligibility because deportation is likely; the court should explain that the non-parole period was not increased because of it. Deportation is relevant only on evidence of its likely risk and impact; without evidence or a prosecution concession it need not be considered.
test: (1) The head sentence is shortened or lengthened because of expected parole, remissions or other executive action, or speculation that parole may be cancelled → error (considering parole prospects when fixing the non-parole period → pass, with the caution of flag.parole_consideration_3_3_3_vs_8_3_3_2). (2) The sentence is adjusted because of registration or working-with-children consequences → error. (3) The sentence is lowered to avoid visa cancellation → error. (4) Parole eligibility denied, or the non-parole period lengthened, because deportation is likely → error; where deportation is in issue and the reasoning does not say the non-parole period was not increased because of it → caution. (5) Deportation hardship given weight without evidence of its likelihood and impact (or a prosecution concession) → caution.
message: The reasoning relies on a consequence the court must disregard or treat with caution (VSM 7.6.2.7, 7.7.2, 8.3.3.2, 8.3.4).

refs.q: The Act prohibits a court from considering the possibility or likelihood that the length of time spent in custody ‘will be affected by executive action of any kind’.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 8 – Imprisonment > 8.3 – Non-parole period > 8.3.3 – Special considerations > 8.3.3.2 – Parole eligibility

refs.q: In fixing a non-parole period, the court must consider that the offender may have to serve every day of the head sentence.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 8 – Imprisonment > 8.3 – Non-parole period > 8.3.3 – Special considerations > 8.3.3.2 – Parole eligibility

refs.q: However, a court may consider the possibility of release on parole, the rehabilitative potential of parole, and the offender’s suitability for parole in fixing a non-parole period.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 8 – Imprisonment > 8.3 – Non-parole period > 8.3.3 – Special considerations > 8.3.3.2 – Parole eligibility

refs.q: A sentencing court is not to consider any consequence that may arise under the Sex Offenders Registration Act 2004 (Vic) or the Working With Children Act 2005 (Vic) from the imposition of sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.7 – Punishment from ancillary orders > 7.7.2 – Punishment in registration as sexual offender

refs.q: As noted, the Migration Act may make visa cancellation mandatory and it does so if an offender is sentenced to one year of imprisonment or more (unless the relevant Minister is satisfied there is a reason to revoke the cancellation). It is, however, error for a sentencing court to artificially lower a sentence in order to avoid the consequences of the Migration Act.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

refs.q: There must also be evidence of both the likely risk of deportation and the impact of that risk. Specifically, the evidence must be ‘sufficient to permit a sensible quantification of that risk to be undertaken’. A reduction will be permissible and appropriate where the prospect of deportation (and its impact) is certain. It may also be appropriate where deportation and its adverse impacts are probable.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

refs.q: Without evidence or a prosecution concession, a court need not consider the possibility of deportation. However, when mandatory cancellation of an offender’s visa under the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) is triggered by the sentence imposed, the potential for their deportation is elevated and this lifts that consideration above being a completely speculative possibility.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 7 – Policy considerations > 7.6 – Hardship of sanction > 7.6.2 – Hardship of imprisonment > 7.6.2.7 – Deportation

refs.q: An offender must not be denied eligibility for parole on the basis they are likely to be deported or transferred interstate on the expiration of any minimum term.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 8 – Imprisonment > 8.3 – Non-parole period > 8.3.4 – Process

refs.q: However, as deportation or transfer may be relevant to an offender’s prospects of rehabilitation, a court may consider it for that purpose but should be careful to explain that the length of the non-parole period has not been increased because of this possibility.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 8 – Imprisonment > 8.3 – Non-parole period > 8.3.4 – Process

title: Victim impact, victim attitude, victim conduct and domestic context
statement: A victim impact statement informs the court of impact but is not to be used to punish or to produce an unjust sentence; a victim’s attitude to sentence is generally irrelevant (forgiveness may show lessened harm, treated with extreme caution in family violence); a victim’s failure to make a statement or take part is not mitigating; victim conduct, if established on the balance of probabilities, may bear on sentence but should not be labelled mitigating or “complicit”. Offending in a domestic context can never be mitigating and may be aggravating.
test: (1) The absence of a victim impact statement or of victim participation treated as mitigating → error. (2) A domestic context treated as mitigating → error. (3) The victim’s wishes about the sentence drive the estimate; forgiveness in family violence given weight without caution; victim conduct relied on without being established on the balance of probabilities; the victim called “complicit” → caution.
message: Check how victim material was used (VSM 2.3.2.2.4, 5.2.6).

refs.q: The statement is not to be used to punish the offender, to produce an unjust or unfair sentence, or to provide background and context.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.3 – Findings > 2.3.2 – Evidence > 2.3.2.2 – Records, depositions, reports, and statements > 2.3.2.2.4 – Statements

refs.q: Generally, a victim’s attitude regarding the sentence to be imposed is irrelevant. But in appropriate cases their forgiveness may indicate that the effects of the offending have not been long lasting and that their suffering is lessened.

title: Parsimony, imprisonment as last resort, the Boulton question and the purposes of a CCO
statement: The sentence must be no more severe than necessary to achieve the purposes; imprisonment may be imposed only if the purposes cannot be achieved by a less severe sentence. For Victorian offences the Boulton question asks whether any feature of the offence or offender requires imprisonment given that a CCO could run for years with punitive and rehabilitative conditions; but the court need not give reasons for rejecting a non-custodial term, failing to ask the question does not by itself show error, and a CCO need not be expressly ruled out. A positive CCO assessment does not presume a CCO. It is erroneous to assume that in a combination sentence the imprisonment deals with punishment and the CCO only with rehabilitation, that the head sentence reflects punishment and the non-parole period rehabilitation, or that a CCO is entirely rehabilitative; equally, there will be cases where a CCO cannot adequately punish.
test: (1) Imprisonment treated as presumptive, or the reasoning shows no consideration of whether the purposes could be met by a less severe sentence → error. (2) A combination sentence reasoned as imprisonment-for-punishment and CCO-for-rehabilitation; the head sentence and non-parole period split between punitive and rehabilitative purposes; a CCO treated as wholly rehabilitative → error. (3) (app policy) Imprisonment proposed where a CCO is legally available but the reasoning does not identify the feature(s) of the offence or offender that require imprisonment → caution. (4) A CCO proposed whose length is not justified on the assumption that every day is served → caution.
message: The reasoning should show that a less severe sentence was considered (VSM 3.2, 8.1); explaining why a CCO would not do is app policy, not a Manual requirement; keep the purposes of each component together (VSM 4.3, 11.7.2, 11.7.5, 11.8.1).

refs.q: It is a common law rule that requires the sentence be no more severe than is necessary to achieve the sentencing purposes. Although often concerned with the type of sanction to be imposed, parsimony also applies to the length of the sanction.

title: Proportionality: neither excessively lenient nor overly severe
statement: The sentence must be proportionate to the gravity of the offence in light of its objective circumstances; a longer term may not be imposed merely to cure a condition, protect the community or detain preventively; proportionality applies to every component, including the total effective sentence. There is no single proportionate sentence, and sentencing is not a stepped process that first fixes a proportionate term. The statutory power to depart from proportionality should be exercised sparingly, with adequate reasons.
test: (1) The sentence is increased for treatment, cure or protection beyond a proportionate term outside the statutory regimes → error. (2) A factor is used to go below what gravity requires without reasons → caution. (3) The reasoning first fixes “the” proportionate term and then adjusts it → caution (and see audit.instinctive_synthesis_not_two_tier). (4) A departure from proportionality under a statutory regime without adequate reasons → caution.
message: Check proportionality of the estimate (VSM 3.1, 4.4).

refs.q: The principle of proportionality defines the upper and lower limits of punishment. It constrains both excessively lenient and overly severe responses to crime.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: It is a well-established principle that says that the sentence imposed should be proportionate to the gravity of the offence considered in the light of the circumstances, including the maximum statutory penalty for the offence, the degree of harm, the method of committing the offence, and the offender’s culpability.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: The maximum penalty, however, is only a guidepost for fixing an appropriate sentence, and a lengthy term cannot be imposed merely to cure an offender’s condition (including drug addiction), to protect the community or to further preventative detention (even in cases of terrorism).
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: The proportionality principle applies to all aspects of sentencing, including the total effective sentence, parity, mitigation, aggregation, cumulation, and the fixing of a non-parole period or suspended sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: There is no single proportionate sentence and an attempt to fix one before fixing the sentence to be imposed will only multiply the possibilities of error.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: Lastly, sentencing is not a stepped process that first requires a court to set a term proportionate to the crime.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

refs.q: the power to depart from it should be exercised sparingly, with adequate reasons given for any decision to do so.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.1 – Proportionality

title: Totality: individual sentences, then cumulation, then stand back; no crushing sentence
statement: The total must be a just and appropriate measure of the total criminality: preferably appropriate individual terms, then concurrency or partial cumulation, then stand back; shortcuts cause error. Where the preferred approach cannot be followed, the secondary “moderate and cumulate” approach may be used. Totality applies to offences cumulated on an existing custodial sentence. A crushing sentence should not be imposed absent special circumstances, but it is wrong to fix a minimum by the need to ensure “some measure of life after release”. For an aggregate sentence the individual sentences need not be announced. Where legislation presumes cumulation, totality must not be applied inconsistently with it.
test: (1) A total is stated without individual sentences and cumulation steps, other than for an aggregate sentence → error. (2) The minimum term is fixed by the need to ensure “some measure of life after release” → error. (3) Individual sentences reduced and then cumulated without saying why the preferred approach could not be followed → caution. (4) Existing sentences being served are ignored in testing totality → caution. (5) The total may be crushing (age, length) without special circumstances → caution (flag.crushing_sentence_principle; whether crushing is assessed within totality: flag.crushing_within_totality). (6) For a serious offender, concurrency directed simply to achieve totality → caution (flag.serious_offender_cumulation_totality).
message: Show the individual sentences and cumulation and test the total (VSM 3.3.1, 3.3.2.1, 3.3.5, 3.5, 8.5).

refs.q: The totality principle requires a court in sentencing an offender for multiple offences to ensure that the aggregate term it imposes is ‘a just and appropriate measure of the total criminality involved’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: To fashion an appropriate total effective head term that satisfies the requirements of totality, it is preferable to impose appropriate individual terms, which satisfy all the sentencing objectives, and then make them wholly or partially concurrent, ‘rather than by an order or orders for the cumulation of unnecessarily reduced individual sentences’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: • Determine an appropriate term for each charge, taking the applicable sentencing considerations into account, and designate the highest term as the base sentence. • Determine the extent to which there should be cumulation regarding each count. • Then ‘stand back’ and consider, in light of the totality principle, what is an appropriate total effective sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: Problems with the application of totality arise when shortcuts are adopted to give effect to the principle.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.5 – Challenges in application

refs.q: Where it is not possible to follow the preferred approach, a court may follow the secondary ‘moderate and cumulate’ approach of imposing reduced individual terms and then cumulating a portion of each to produce an appropriate total effective sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: The totality principle applies when sentencing for offences that may overlap or be cumulated upon an existing custodial sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.1 – Purpose and approaches

refs.q: A court should not impose a ‘crushing sentence’ unless there are special circumstances.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: It is wrong, however, to determine a minimum sentence by the need to ensure ‘some measure of life after release’.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.5 – Avoidance of a crushing sentence

refs.q: However, the court does not have to identify the separate events giving rise to the specific charges or to announce the sentences it would have imposed for each offence if separate sentences had been imposed, or whether they would have been imposed concurrently or cumulatively.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 8 – Imprisonment > 8.5 – Aggregate sentence

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.2 – Legislative interaction > 3.3.2.1 – Victoria

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.3 – Totality > 3.3.3 – Application to parole

title: Parity with co-offenders
statement: Any significant difference between co-offenders’ sentences must be capable of rational explanation (age, background, history, role; plea timing does not by itself justify a marked disparity); all components including non-parole periods are compared; using a co-offender’s sentence as a starting point and adjusting it is an inappropriate two-step process; where parity requires modification, err on the side of leniency — but an excessively lenient co-offender sentence cannot justify an inappropriately low one. Parity has only limited application between offenders sentenced under different systems (e.g. adult and juvenile).
test: If a co-offender’s sentence is supplied: (1) the reasoning starts from the co-offender’s sentence and adjusts it → error. (2) A difference is not explained by identified differences → caution. (3) Only head sentences are compared → caution. (4) An excessively lenient co-offender sentence used to reduce the estimate to an inappropriately low level → caution. (5) Parity applied with full force across adult and juvenile systems → caution.
message: Explain the relationship with the co-offender’s sentence (VSM 2.1.1, 3.6, 3.6.1).

refs.q: The concept is simply that when two or more co-offenders are sentenced, any significant difference in the sentences imposed upon them should be capable of a rational explanation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: However, the willingness of one offender to plead guilty earlier than another co-offender, does not justify a ‘marked’ disparity in sentences between the two;
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Comparison of the head sentence alone is not an adequate measure of parity. All components of the sentence (including any non-parole period) must be considered, and if totality requires different sentences between the co-offenders, then parity is not breached.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Where parity does require modification of the sentence to be imposed, it is appropriate to err on the side of leniency and eliminate or diminish the appearance of injustice by reducing the more severe penalty, even where it is otherwise appropriate and within the permissible range of sentencing options.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Although there is no dictated sentencing sequence, using the sentence of a co-offender as a starting point and then reducing or increasing the sentence being imposed based on other factors is an inappropriate two-step process.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: But an excessively lenient sentence cannot justify the reduction of a co-offender’s sentence to an inappropriately low level.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

refs.q: Parity has only a limited application to these offenders because they are sentenced under different systems where different principles apply.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 3 – Sentencing principles > 3.6 – Parity

title: Young offenders: rehabilitation emphasis; CYFA considerations for children; youth detention; adult minimums regarded
statement: For youthful offenders rehabilitation is usually far more important than general deterrence, though the weight of youth decreases as the seriousness of the offence increases; a youthful first offender should not, if avoidable, be given a custodial sentence; youth detention is available in the higher courts for young offenders. For a child sentenced in the Supreme or County Court the CYFA considerations must be addressed as far as practicable, and the CYFA dispositions are considered in their hierarchy (the Manual notes some ambiguity about the higher courts’ power); in CNK v The Queen a child before the higher court only because of a charge of which he was acquitted had to be sentenced on the remaining uplifted charges as if exclusively governed by the CYFA (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges). The higher courts, sentencing an offender aged 16 or 17 at the time of an indictable offence, must have regard to the adult minimum non-parole provisions when assessing gravity.
test: Trigger (app assumption): the offender was under 21 at the offence or at sentence. (1) Youth is not discussed → error. (2) A child sentenced in the Supreme or County Court: the CYFA considerations are not addressed, or the CYFA dispositions are not considered first in their hierarchy, or a youth attendance, youth control, YRC or YJC order is made without a conviction → error; whether the higher court may impose a CYFA disposition → caution (flag.cyfa_disposition_power). (3) Aged 16 or 17 at an indictable offence sentenced in a higher court where an adult minimum would apply: no regard to it shown → error. (4) General deterrence relied on heavily for a child → error, unless the reasoning finds that punishment beyond the CYFA (or s 32(3)(b)), or adult custody, is necessary — then → caution (as (7): flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges; audit.purposes_balance). (5) Custody proposed without considering youth detention where available → caution. (6) Youth given decisive weight for the gravest offending without considering that its weight decreases with seriousness → caution. (7) Charges that might have been dealt with in the Children’s Court are dealt with in a superior court and general deterrence is relied on → caution: the Manual says it is unclear whether general deterrence applies, and likely does only if punishment beyond the CYFA (or s 32(3)(b)) is necessary — the reasoning should say whether that is so (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges). (8) A child before the Supreme or County Court only because of a charge of which they were acquitted (CNK; intake.court) is sentenced to a disposition outside the CYFA → caution (flag.general_deterrence_childrens_court_charges); not known → no limb.

refs.q: General deterrence has minimal relevance when sentencing a child.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: For youthful offenders, rehabilitation is usually far more important than general deterrence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: The weight to be given to an offender’s youth and their rehabilitation decreases as the seriousness of the offence for which they are to be sentenced increases.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

refs.q: A youthful first offender should not, if it can be avoided, be given a custodial sentence.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation

refs.q: Regardless of the charge, if a custodial sentence is deemed appropriate for a young offender on conviction (or appeal) in a higher court, that court may make a youth justice centre order (‘YJC’) or a youth residential centre order (‘YRC’). refs.q: In determining an appropriate sentence, a reviewing court must, ‘as far as practicable,’ consider: • the need to strengthen and preserve the relationship between the child and their family; • the desirability of allowing the child to live at home; • the desirability of allowing the education, training or employment of the child to continue; • the need to minimise stigma to the child; • the suitability of the sentence to the child; • if appropriate, the need to ensure that the child is aware they must bear responsibility for any illegal action by them; • the need to protect the community, or any person, from violent or other wrongful acts of the child — • in all cases where the sentence is for a Category A serious youth offence or a Category B serious youth offence; or • in any other case — if it is appropriate to do so; and • if appropriate, the need to deter the child from offending in remand centres, youth residential centres or youth justice centres.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 10 – Youth and youth detention > 10.1 – Legislative regime > 10.1.2 – Sentencing children in adult courts

refs.q: The Court of Appeal has held that ‘as far as practicable’ are terms of emphases that mean the sentencing court ‘must have regard to each of the listed considerations to the maximum extent possible’.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 10 – Youth and youth detention > 10.1 – Legislative regime > 10.1.2 – Sentencing children in adult courts

refs.q: It is only for the gravest offending where the offender has almost no prospect of rehabilitation, that youth may not be a mitigating factor.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 10 – Youth and youth detention > 10.1 – Legislative regime > 10.1.2 – Sentencing children in adult courts > 10.1.2.1 – Interaction with sentencing principles and purposes

refs.q: Meaning a court may not impose a sentence in a given paragraph of the following list unless it is first satisfied that it is not appropriate to impose one given in any preceding paragraph.

The dispositions available under the CYFA, in ascending hierarchical order, are: • dismissing the charge, without conviction; • dismissing the charge and ordering the giving of an undertaking, without conviction; • dismissing the charge and ordering the giving of an accountable undertaking, without conviction; • placing the child on a good behaviour bond, without conviction; • imposing a fine, with or without conviction; • placing the child on probation, with or without conviction; • releasing the child on a youth supervision order, with or without conviction; • convicting the child and making a youth attendance order; • convicting the child and making a youth control order; • convicting the child and making a YRC order; • convicting child and making YJC order.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 10 – Youth and youth detention > 10.1 – Legislative regime > 10.1.2 – Sentencing children in adult courts

refs.q: Although not without ambiguity, it appears that the Supreme Court or County Court may impose a sentence under the CYFA or, if it concludes that the dispositions available under the CYFA are inadequate, may impose any sentence available under the Act.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 10 – Youth and youth detention > 10.1 – Legislative regime > 10.1.2 – Sentencing children in adult courts

refs.q: Lastly, Parliament requires the higher courts in sentencing an offender aged 16 years or more but under 18 years at the time of the commission of an indictable offence, to ‘have regard to any requirement in [the] Act that a specified minimum non-parole period…be fixed or a specified minimum term of imprisonment be imposed, had that offence been committed by an adult’.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 10 – Youth and youth detention > 10.1 – Legislative regime > 10.1.2 – Sentencing children in adult courts

refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.2 – Deterrence > 4.2.1 – General deterrence

title: Recording a conviction; dismissals, discharges and adjournments
statement: Whether to record a conviction depends on all the circumstances including the nature of the offence, character and history, and the impact on economic or social wellbeing or employment; for serious offending, not recording a conviction is limited to out of the ordinary or exceptional circumstances that facilitate the offender’s rehabilitation. The Manual says a dismissed offence must be capable of being characterised as trifling, and also that dismissals may be granted for strong rehabilitative steps or where good character and post-offence conduct would make a conviction disproportionate. (Conviction requirements for imprisonment, youth detention and discharge are hard-checked by audit.conviction_requirements.)
test: If a non-conviction order is proposed: (1) the statutory factors are not addressed → caution; (2) for serious offending, no out of the ordinary or exceptional circumstances that facilitate the offender’s rehabilitation are identified → caution; (3) a dismissal proposed: state whether the offence is trifling or which alternative ground is relied on → caution (flag.dismissal_trifling_requirement).
message: Check the basis for not recording a conviction (VSM 2.4.1, 4.3.1, 13, 13.1).

refs.q: In deciding whether to record a conviction, a court must consider all the circumstances of the case including the nature of the offence, the character and history of the offender, and the impact of recording a conviction on their economic or social well-being, or employment prospects.
refs.path: Part A – Method and Process > 2 – Method and process > 2.4 – Imposition of sentence > 2.4.1 – Defining ‘sentence’

refs.q: A court also has the discretion not to record a conviction, though the exercise of this in cases of serious offending will be limited to ‘out of the ordinary’ or ‘exceptional’ circumstances that facilitate an offender’s rehabilitation.
refs.path: Part B – Principles, Purposes and Considerations > 4 – Sentencing purposes > 4.3 – Rehabilitation > 4.3.1 – Non-custodial sentences and non-conviction dispositions

refs.q: Moreover, the offence must be of such a nature that it can properly be characterised as ‘trifling’. The circumstances must clearly indicate that it would be manifestly unfair and unreasonable to penalise an offender and impose the stigma of a conviction.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.1 – Dismissals

refs.q: Dismissals may also be granted where strong steps have been taken towards rehabilitation, or where previous good character and post-offence conduct would make a conviction disproportionate to the crime.
refs.path: Part C – Sanctions > 13 – Dismissals, discharges, and adjournments > 13.1 – Dismissals

title: Confiscation and compensation: effect on sentence and priority
statement: The Act distinguishes orders disgorging the profits of crime, which are not to be considered, from forfeiture of lawfully acquired property or a pecuniary penalty exceeding the profits, which may be; it prohibits taking into account the automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property. Confiscation that does more than remove profits is punishment and failing to consider it may be error, but there must be sufficient evidence of its likely effect. Compensation orders cannot be a CCO condition, and where the offender cannot pay both a fine and compensation, compensation must be given priority.
test: (1) Mitigation given for an order disgorging profits, or for the automatic forfeiture of a serious drug offender’s property → error. (2) A compensation order made a condition of a CCO → error. (3) A fine given priority over compensation where the offender cannot pay both → error. (4) Punitive confiscation shown on the evidence (lawfully acquired property, or a pecuniary penalty beyond the profits) ignored → caution. (5) Means assessed without accounting for forfeiture, restitution and compensation orders → caution (audit.fine_reasoning).

title: Reasons show the route to the conclusion; unusual features explained; references cited
statement: Reasons should usually state the findings of fact and their basis, the aggravating and mitigating factors, the impact on victims, the offender’s material circumstances and conclusions on the primary arguments — the route to the conclusion; an unusual factor that may carry weight (such as an unusual non-parole period) should be explained; statutory matters discussed rather than recited; intemperate or formulaic language avoided. Where there is a duty to give reasons, failure to do so is an error of law (the statutory statements are hard-checked elsewhere). Before a CCO or an adjourned undertaking the court must explain the order’s purposes, effect and consequences to the offender.

title: Category 2 residual exception and “special reasons”: the restricted reasoning
statement: The Category 2 residual exception is a stringent, non-discretionary test: are there substantial and compelling circumstances, and are they exceptional and rare? In applying it general deterrence and denunciation must be given primacy, personal circumstances less weight than the gravity of the offending, and regard must not be had to previous good character, an early guilty plea, prospects of rehabilitation or parity. For a mandatory minimum, a special reason may exist in four circumstances; for the residual “substantial and compelling reasons” the court must give primacy to general deterrence and denunciation, must not consider prior good character (other than an absence of prior convictions), an early plea, rehabilitation prospects or parity, and must have regard to Parliament’s intention that a custodial term should ordinarily be imposed. The offender carries the burden; the impairment ground must be proved on the balance of probabilities.
test: Whenever the estimate relies on the Category 2 residual exception or a special reason: (1) good character, an early plea, rehabilitation prospects or parity is counted towards the exception → error (for the treatment of a lack of prior convictions under the two tests → caution: flag.good_character_category2_vs_special_reason). (2) General deterrence and denunciation are not given primacy, or personal circumstances outweigh gravity → error. (3) The circumstances are not shown to be both substantial and compelling and exceptional and rare (residual tests) → error. (4) The impairment ground is relied on without evidence proving it on the balance of probabilities → error. (5) The reasoning does not acknowledge that the offender carries the burden → caution. (6) A special reason relied on to avoid imprisonment for a Category 1 offence that carries no mandatory minimum → error (no special reason exists for it: 9.1.3; audit.category_1_2 (d)).

title: Fines: decide whether to fine before considering means; no harsher sentence for inability to pay
statement: An offender’s financial circumstances can be considered only after deciding to impose a fine; they are irrelevant to whether a fine should be imposed. A court should not impose a more severe sentence, such as imprisonment, because the offender cannot pay a fine that properly reflects the gravity of the offence. A fine beyond the offender’s reasonable capacity to pay is never just; the onus is on the offender to put material before the court about means, and capacity to pay is relevant but not dominant. Forfeiture, restitution and compensation orders must be taken into account. A fine with imprisonment may require the term to be reduced, and should not be imposed where default is likely.
test: (1) Means used to decide whether to impose a fine → error. (2) A more severe sentence proposed because the offender cannot pay an appropriate fine → error. (3) A fine set beyond the offender’s reasonable capacity to pay as shown on the facts → caution. (4) A fine added to imprisonment without considering the combined effect or the likelihood of default → caution. (5) Compensation’s bearing on whether to fine → caution (flag.compensation_whether_to_fine).

title: Licence disqualification: the period reasoned, interaction with other sanctions, earlier suspensions
statement: Fixing a disqualification period is like the general sentencing discretion: aggravating and mitigating factors and the competing principles and purposes must be considered; a failure to give reasons for the period may indicate error; its effect on rehabilitation must be considered, and its interaction with other sanctions and its actual impact on the offender should be considered; failure to consider that interaction and impact may be error. A later suspension under the same specified provisions is presumed concurrent with the earlier one unless the court orders otherwise or the RSA requires the suspension or disqualification to be consecutive; and where the licence or permit has been suspended under Part 6B of the Road Safety Act and the court cancels and disqualifies, or suspends, it must take that period of suspension into account in fixing the period.
test: (1) An earlier suspension under Part 6B of the RSA (on the stated facts) is not taken into account in fixing the period of suspension or disqualification → error. (2) The period’s effect on rehabilitation is not considered at all → error (16.5 “must consider”). (2a) The period is stated without reasons, or without considering its interaction with other sanctions and the impact on the person → caution (16.5: “may indicate error”, “may constitute error”). (3) A later suspension under the same provisions treated as cumulative on an earlier one without an order saying so, and no RSA requirement of consecutive periods identified → caution.
